practice.stem: A student drops a bar magnet vertically through a coil of wire connected to a data-logger. It is suggested that the maximum e.m.f. E induced in the coil is related to the height h from which the magnet is released above the coil by E = k hⁿ, where k and n are constants.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between E and h. Explain how your results could be used to determine the values of k and n. You should draw a labelled diagram (describe it in words here) showing the arrangement of your apparatus. In your account you should pay particular attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.answer: Vary h; measure peak E with a data-logger or oscilloscope; keep the same magnet, coil (turns, area) and orientation; release from rest through a tube to keep it vertical; plot lg E against lg h: gradient = n, y-intercept = lg k.
parts.working: Mark points: independent variable h, dependent variable E (B1); control: same magnet/strength, same coil (number of turns, area), magnet passes through same point/same orientation (B1, B1). Measure h with a metre rule from bottom of magnet to top of coil (B1); connect coil to data-logger/CRO, read the peak e.m.f. from the trace (B1); release magnet from rest, use a vertical plastic tube as a guide (B1). Plot lg E against lg h (B1); n = gradient, k = 10^(y-intercept) (B1). Safety: use a soft landing (sand tray/foam) so the falling magnet does not break or hit feet (B1). Detail: use a set-square to check the tube is vertical; repeat each h and average peak E; use a high data-logging rate; check the straight line confirms the relationship; keep magnet away from steel; avoid magnet touching the tube sides (D1 each, max 6). Marks are awarded for: defining the problem (independent and dependent variables, key control variable(s)) – 3; methods of data collection (workable apparatus/circuit, how each quantity is measured) – 3; method of analysis (graph to plot, how the constant is found) – 2; safety (specific to this set-up) – 1; additional detail – up to 6. Total 15.

practice.stem: A flat circular coil carries a constant current. It is suggested that the magnetic flux density B at the centre of the coil is related to the radius r of the coil by B = k/r, where k is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between B and r. Explain how your results could be used to determine a value for k. You should draw a labelled diagram (describe it in words here) showing the arrangement of your apparatus. In your account you should pay particular attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.answer: Make coils of the same number of turns but different radii (wind round cylinders of known diameter); keep current constant with a variable resistor and ammeter; measure B at the centre with a calibrated Hall probe; plot B against 1/r: straight line through origin, gradient = k.
parts.working: Mark points: independent r, dependent B (B1); control: same current, same number of turns (B1). Circuit: d.c. supply, ammeter, rheostat in series with coil (B1); Hall probe at the centre, plane of probe perpendicular to field/along axis (B1); measure diameter with a metre rule or calipers and halve it (B1); use the Hall probe calibrated (or zero it away from the coil) (B1). Plot B against 1/r (B1); k = gradient, relationship valid if straight line through origin (B1). Safety: coil may get hot – switch off between readings / do not touch the coil (B1). Detail: adjust rheostat to keep current constant; take the probe reading with current reversed and average to remove Earth's field; measure diameter in several directions; use a large current for a large B, but avoid overheating; mount the probe in a clamp so its position is fixed (D1 each, max 6). Marks are awarded for: defining the problem (independent and dependent variables, key control variable(s)) – 3; methods of data collection (workable apparatus/circuit, how each quantity is measured) – 3; method of analysis (graph to plot, how the constant is found) – 2; safety (specific to this set-up) – 1; additional detail – up to 6. Total 15.

practice.stem: A coil of resistance wire is placed in a beaker of water and a current I passes through it for a fixed time. It is suggested that the rise in temperature Δθ of the water is related to I by Δθ = kI², where k is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between Δθ and I. Explain how your results could be used to determine a value for k. You should draw a labelled diagram (describe it in words here) showing the arrangement of your apparatus. In your account you should pay particular attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.answer: Vary I with a rheostat; heat the same mass of water for the same time; measure starting and final temperatures with a thermometer; plot Δθ against I²: straight line through origin, gradient = k.
parts.working: Mark points: independent I, dependent Δθ (B1); control: same mass/volume of water, same heating time, same coil/wire (B1). Circuit: low-voltage d.c. supply, ammeter in series, rheostat (B1); thermometer (or temperature sensor) in water, initial and final readings, stir (B1); measure time with a stopwatch, measure mass of water with a balance (B1); fresh water at same starting temperature each time (B1). Plot Δθ against I² (B1); k = gradient, valid if straight line through origin (B1). Safety: coil may be hot – allow to cool/use tongs; keep electrical connections dry (B1). Detail: insulate/lag the beaker and use a lid; read highest temperature after switching off; keep current constant during heating by adjusting rheostat; insulated wire so current does not pass through the water; repeat and average; choose times giving Δθ of several degrees (D1 each, max 6). Marks are awarded for: defining the problem (independent and dependent variables, key control variable(s)) – 3; methods of data collection (workable apparatus/circuit, how each quantity is measured) – 3; method of analysis (graph to plot, how the constant is found) – 2; safety (specific to this set-up) – 1; additional detail – up to 6. Total 15.

practice.stem: An alternating current of constant amplitude in a long solenoid induces an e.m.f. in a small search coil placed inside it. It is suggested that the peak e.m.f. E₀ induced in the search coil is related to the frequency f of the current by E₀ = kf, where k is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between E₀ and f. Explain how your results could be used to determine a value for k. You should draw a labelled diagram (describe it in words here) showing the arrangement of your apparatus. In your account you should pay particular attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.answer: Use a signal generator to drive the solenoid, with an a.c. ammeter to keep the current amplitude constant; place the search coil at the centre, coaxial; measure peak e.m.f. on an oscilloscope (Y-gain × peak height); find f from the generator or CRO time-base; plot E₀ against f: gradient = k.
parts.working: Mark points: independent f, dependent E₀ (B1); control: same current amplitude in solenoid, same position and orientation of search coil (B1). Circuit: signal generator (a.c. source) connected to solenoid with a.c. ammeter in series (B1); search coil connected to CRO (B1); E₀ = vertical height of peak × Y-gain (B1); f from signal generator dial or period from time-base, f = 1/T (B1). Plot E₀ against f (B1); k = gradient, valid if straight line through origin (B1). Safety: solenoid may become hot at large currents – switch off between readings (B1). Detail: coil axis parallel to solenoid axis; centre of solenoid where field uniform; adjust generator output to keep current constant at each f; use wide frequency range (e.g. 100 Hz – 5 kHz); measure peak-to-peak and halve; repeat each reading (D1 each, max 6). Marks are awarded for: defining the problem (independent and dependent variables, key control variable(s)) – 3; methods of data collection (workable apparatus/circuit, how each quantity is measured) – 3; method of analysis (graph to plot, how the constant is found) – 2; safety (specific to this set-up) – 1; additional detail – up to 6. Total 15.

practice.stem: A capacitor of capacitance C is charged and then discharged through a fixed resistor of resistance R. It is suggested that the time t½ for the potential difference across the capacitor to fall to half of its initial value is related to C by t½ = RC ln 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between t½ and C. Explain how your results could be used to determine a value for R and to test the relationship. You should draw a labelled diagram (describe it in words here) showing the arrangement of your apparatus. In your account you should pay particular attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.answer: Charge capacitors of different C (use a range, e.g. in parallel combinations) from a d.c. supply with a two-way switch; discharge through the same R; measure V against time with a voltmeter/data-logger and find t½; plot t½ against C: straight line through origin, gradient = R ln 2 so R = gradient/ln 2.
parts.working: Mark points: independent C, dependent t½ (B1); control: same resistor R, same initial charging p.d. (B1); circuit: d.c. supply, two-way switch, capacitor, resistor, voltmeter across capacitor (B1, B1); time with stopwatch started as switch moved or use data-logger to record V–t and read time for V₀/2 (B1); determine C from labelled values or measure with capacitance meter (B1). Plot t½ against C (B1); relationship valid if straight line through origin, R = gradient/ln 2 (B1). Safety: electrolytic capacitors connected the right way round/not exceeding rated voltage, discharge before handling (B1). Detail: choose large R (e.g. ≥ 10 kΩ) and C (100–1000 µF) so t½ is several seconds; high-resistance voltmeter (digital) so it does not discharge the capacitor; repeat and average t½; measure R with an ohmmeter for comparison; combine capacitors in parallel to vary C; time several halvings or use data-logger at high rate (D1 each, max 6). Marks are awarded for: defining the problem (independent and dependent variables, key control variable(s)) – 3; methods of data collection (workable apparatus/circuit, how each quantity is measured) – 3; method of analysis (graph to plot, how the constant is found) – 2; safety (specific to this set-up) – 1; additional detail – up to 6. Total 15.

practice.stem: It is suggested that the resistance R of a thermistor is related to its thermodynamic temperature T by R = A e^(B/T), where A and B are constants.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between R and T. Explain how your results could be used to determine values for A and B. You should draw a labelled diagram (describe it in words here) showing the arrangement of your apparatus. In your account you should pay particular attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.answer: Heat the thermistor in a water bath; measure the temperature with a thermometer and R with an ohmmeter (or V and I); convert to kelvin; plot ln R against 1/T: gradient = B, y-intercept = ln A.
parts.working: Mark points: independent T, dependent R (B1); control: same thermistor, same current/avoid self-heating (B1). Thermistor in a test tube in a water bath heated by a Bunsen/electric heater, stirred (B1); thermometer next to thermistor (B1); R measured with ohmmeter, or ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel with R = V/I (B1); convert θ to T = θ + 273 (B1). Plot ln R against 1/T (B1); B = gradient, A = e^(y-intercept) (B1). Safety: hot water – use tongs/gloves, place apparatus on a stable surface (B1). Detail: waterproof the thermistor leads (plastic tube or sealed bag); stir and wait for thermal equilibrium before each reading; heat slowly/switch off heater while reading; use ice-water and boiling water to give a wide range; small current to avoid self-heating; repeat with temperature falling and average (D1 each, max 6). Marks are awarded for: defining the problem (independent and dependent variables, key control variable(s)) – 3; methods of data collection (workable apparatus/circuit, how each quantity is measured) – 3; method of analysis (graph to plot, how the constant is found) – 2; safety (specific to this set-up) – 1; additional detail – up to 6. Total 15.

practice.stem: A mass hanging on a spring oscillates vertically. A thin card of area S is attached horizontally to the mass so that air resistance damps the oscillations. The amplitude A decreases with time t according to A = A₀ e^(−λt). It is suggested that λ = c Sᵖ, where c and p are constants.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between λ and S. Explain how your results could be used to determine the values of c and p. You should draw a labelled diagram (describe it in words here) showing the arrangement of your apparatus. In your account you should pay particular attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.answer: For each card area, record the amplitude against time (e.g. motion sensor or video with a scale); find λ from the gradient of ln A against t; vary S using square cards of different side; plot lg λ against lg S: gradient = p, intercept = lg c.
parts.working: Mark points: independent S, dependent λ (B1); control: same total oscillating mass (card + mass), same spring, same initial amplitude (B1). Measure S by measuring card sides with a ruler (B1); determine A at intervals using a motion sensor below the mass/data-logger, or video with a vertical metre rule and frame timer (B1); find λ: plot ln A against t, λ = −gradient (B1); repeat for several areas (B1). Plot lg λ against lg S (B1); p = gradient, c = 10^(y-intercept) (B1). Safety: keep feet clear in case the mass falls / clamp stand secured with a G-clamp (B1). Detail: add balancing masses so total mass is constant; keep card horizontal (spirit level); small initial amplitude so card stays horizontal; no draughts; use a fiducial marker; repeat each λ; use lightweight stiff card (D1 each, max 6). Marks are awarded for: defining the problem (independent and dependent variables, key control variable(s)) – 3; methods of data collection (workable apparatus/circuit, how each quantity is measured) – 3; method of analysis (graph to plot, how the constant is found) – 2; safety (specific to this set-up) – 1; additional detail – up to 6. Total 15.

practice.stem: A stretched steel wire of fixed length vibrates at its fundamental frequency f when it carries an alternating current and is placed between the poles of a magnet. It is suggested that f is related to the tension T in the wire by f = c Tⁿ, where c and n are constants.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between f and T. Explain how your results could be used to determine the values of c and n. You should draw a labelled diagram (describe it in words here) showing the arrangement of your apparatus. In your account you should pay particular attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.answer: Hang masses from the wire over a pulley to set the tension (T = mg); keep the vibrating length fixed between two bridges, magnet at the centre; adjust the signal generator frequency until the amplitude is a maximum (resonance); plot lg f against lg T: gradient = n, intercept = lg c.
parts.working: Mark points: independent T, dependent f (B1); control: same wire (material, diameter), same length between bridges (B1). Tension from hanging masses over a pulley, T = mg (B1); wire connected to a signal generator; magnet placed at the centre of the vibrating length (B1); vary frequency until a large-amplitude single loop is seen and record f from the generator, or check with a CRO (B1); measure m with a balance (B1). Plot lg f against lg T (B1); n = gradient, c = 10^(y-intercept) (B1). Safety: wire under tension may snap – wear safety goggles; keep feet away from hanging masses / use a box of sand below (B1). Detail: approach resonance from above and below and average; use a small current to avoid heating the wire; fix the length with a metre rule between bridges; use a lightweight paper rider to detect maximum amplitude; repeat readings; check wire is not stretched permanently (D1 each, max 6). Marks are awarded for: defining the problem (independent and dependent variables, key control variable(s)) – 3; methods of data collection (workable apparatus/circuit, how each quantity is measured) – 3; method of analysis (graph to plot, how the constant is found) – 2; safety (specific to this set-up) – 1; additional detail – up to 6. Total 15.

practice.stem: In the experiment of a pendulum with T = 2π√((L + c)/g), a graph of T² against L has gradient 4.05 ± 0.12 s² m⁻¹ and y-intercept 0.122 ± 0.010 s².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine g, with its absolute uncertainty.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine c, with its absolute uncertainty.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the period when L = 1.50 m.

practice.stem: A capacitor discharges through a resistor of resistance 47.0 kΩ ± 5 %. The potential difference V across the capacitor is measured at times t. A graph of ln (V / V) against t / s (V measured in volts, t in seconds) is a straight line with gradient −0.0213 ± 0.0006 s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the capacitance C of the capacitor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the percentage uncertainty in C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the time for the potential difference to fall to one quarter of its initial value.

practice.stem: A student's analysis gives the straight-line relationship y = x/b + a/2, where a and b are constants. Her graph of y against x has gradient 3.00 ± 0.06 and y-intercept 0.25 ± 0.01.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the value of the constant a with its absolute uncertainty.
parts.working: y-intercept = a/2, so a = 2 × 0.25 = 0.50 (B1); the factor 2 is exact, so %Δa = 0.01/0.25 = 4 %, Δa = 0.02 (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the gradient and hence in b.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the value of y when x = 2.50, and state its uncertainty as a percentage, given that x is exact.

practice.subtopic: Analysis: graph, error bars & worst line
practice.stem: A student plots a graph of lg (T/s) against lg (L/m) with error bars in the lg T direction. All values of T have an absolute uncertainty of ± 0.05 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the values of lg (T/s) at the top and bottom of the error bar for the point T = 2.45 ± 0.05 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the values at the ends of the error bar for T = 0.84 ± 0.05 s, and explain why this error bar is longer than the one in (a).
parts.answer: −0.051 and −0.102; same absolute uncertainty is a larger fraction of a smaller value
parts.working: lg 0.89 = −0.051 and lg 0.79 = −0.102 (B1); Δ(lg T) ≈ 0.43ΔT/T, so larger for smaller T (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the worst acceptable straight line should be drawn on this graph.
parts.answer: The steepest or shallowest straight line that passes through all the error bars (usually through the ends of the error bars of the extreme points).

practice.subtopic: Analysis: graph, error bars & worst line
practice.stem: A student plots y against x with error bars in y. The first point is x = 0.010, y = 2.40 ± 0.10 and the last point is x = 0.050, y = 6.30 ± 0.20 (both in consistent units). The intermediate points lie within the error bars of the line joining these two points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the y-values at the top and bottom of the error bars for the first and last points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The worst acceptable line is the steepest line passing through all the error bars. It passes through the bottom of the first error bar and the top of the last. Calculate its gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The best-fit line passes through the first and last data points. Determine the uncertainty in the gradient.

practice.subtopic: Analysis: graph, error bars & worst line

parts.label: a
parts.text: Line L₁ is y = 8.6x + 0.91. Determine, by calculation, whether L₁ passes through every error bar.
parts.answer: Yes – it gives 1.77, 2.63, 3.49, 4.35, 5.21, which all lie within (or at the ends of) the error bars.
parts.working: M1 calculates the y-values from the line at all five x-values; A1 compares with the ranges 1.77–1.93, 2.52–2.72, 3.36–3.60, 4.06–4.36, 4.89–5.21 and concludes yes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Line L₂ is y = 9.0x + 0.85. Determine whether L₂ is an acceptable worst line.
parts.answer: No – at x = 0.10 it gives 1.75, below the error bar (1.77–1.93), and at x = 0.50 it gives 5.35, above the error bar (4.89–5.21).
parts.working: M1 calculation of y from L₂; A1 identifies at least one point whose error bar it misses, so not acceptable

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the worst acceptable line is used rather than simply joining the extreme points.
parts.answer: It shows the largest/smallest gradient consistent with all the data and their uncertainties, giving the uncertainty in the gradient.

practice.stem: On a graph of y against x, the best-fit line passes through (0.20, 1.46) and (0.80, 3.38). The worst acceptable line passes through (0.20, 1.58) and (0.80, 3.30). The x-axis starts at x = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the best-fit line.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the worst acceptable line and hence the uncertainty in the gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the y-intercept of the best-fit line and its uncertainty.

practice.stem: On a graph of y against x, the best-fit line passes through (2.0, −0.35) and (8.0, 1.45). The worst acceptable line passes through (2.0, −0.25) and (8.0, 1.35).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the best-fit line and the y-intercept at x = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the uncertainties in the gradient and in the y-intercept.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The x-axis on the student's graph starts at x = 2.0. Explain why the intercept cannot be read directly from the graph.
parts.answer: The y-axis is not at x = 0 (false origin), so the value where the line crosses it is not the y-intercept; it must be calculated using y = mx + c.

practice.stem: A metre rule is clamped to the bench as a cantilever with a mass fixed to its free end. The period T of vertical oscillation is measured for different lengths L. It is suggested that T = k Lⁿ. A graph of lg (T/s) against lg (L/m) has gradient 1.48 ± 0.04 and y-intercept 0.062 ± 0.012.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the value of n with its uncertainty.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine k and its absolute uncertainty. Give k with its unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your values to predict the period when L = 0.600 m.

practice.stem: Three measurements of the period T of an oscillating rule are 1.34 s, 1.38 s and 1.36 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean value of T with its absolute uncertainty, taking the uncertainty as half the range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate lg (T/s) and its absolute uncertainty.
parts.working: lg 1.36 = 0.134 (B1, 3 d.p. to match 3 s.f.); uncertainty = lg 1.38 − lg 1.36 = 0.006 (B1)

practice.stem: In an experiment, a student uses resistors whose resistance R has a stated tolerance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate 1/R in units of 10⁻³ Ω⁻¹, with its absolute uncertainty, for R = 22 ± 1 Ω and for R = 47 ± 2 Ω.
parts.working: 1/22 = 45.5 × 10⁻³, uncertainty = (ΔR/R) × (1/R) = 2.1 × 10⁻³ → 45 ± 2 (B1); 1/47 = 21.3 × 10⁻³, uncertainty 0.9 × 10⁻³ (B1). Max/min method also accepted (1/21 − 1/22 = 2.2 × 10⁻³)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the absolute uncertainty in 1/R is smaller for the larger resistor even though ΔR is larger.
parts.answer: Absolute uncertainty in 1/R = ΔR/R², and R² increases faster than ΔR.

practice.stem: A cell of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r is connected to a resistance box of resistance R and an ammeter of negligible resistance. The current is I. The relationship is E = I(R + r).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A graph is plotted of 1/I on the y-axis against R on the x-axis. Determine expressions for the gradient and the y-intercept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how E and r are found from the graph.

practice.stem: A pendulum is made from a long string with a large irregular bob. The length L is measured from the support to a mark on the bob. It is suggested that the period T is related to L by T = 2π√((L + c)/g), where c is the unknown distance from the mark to the centre of mass and g is the acceleration of free fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A graph is plotted of T² on the y-axis against L on the x-axis. Determine expressions for the gradient and the y-intercept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how c can be found from the gradient and the y-intercept.

practice.stem: A student times 10 oscillations of a pendulum three times, obtaining 12.46 s, 12.38 s and 12.52 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period T of the pendulum, giving your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
parts.working: mean of 10T = 12.45 s (C1); T = 1.25 s (3 s.f., consistent with raw times) (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student records the length of the pendulum as 65 cm using a metre rule. State why this is not an acceptable record and write a suitable one.
parts.answer: A metre rule reads to the nearest mm, so the length should be recorded to 0.1 cm, e.g. 65.0 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student timed 10 oscillations and repeated the measurement.
parts.answer: To reduce the percentage uncertainty from reaction time and to check for consistency/reduce random error.

practice.stem:
A student records the following table.
L | 1/L
20.0 | 5
35.0 | 2.857142
50 | 2.0
65.0 | 1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two faults in the student's table.
parts.answer: Column headings have no units (should be L / cm and 1/L / m⁻¹); 1/L values are not given to a consistent number of significant figures (and ‘50’ is not recorded to the precision of the rule).
parts.working: B1 each, any two of: missing units/solidus; inconsistent s.f. in calculated column; raw L not to nearest mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate 1/L in m⁻¹ for L = 35.0 cm and L = 65.0 cm, to an appropriate number of significant figures.

practice.subtopic: Graph plotting & line of best fit
practice.stem:
A student obtains these readings.
x / mm: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
y / mm: 12.1, 17.0, 21.9, 29.5, 31.8, 36.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the other five points to show that point (40, 29.5) is anomalous. (The other points lie close to y = 0.495x + 7.09.)
parts.answer: The line predicts y = 26.9 at x = 40, but the reading is 29.5, which is far off the trend of the other points.
parts.working: M1 calculates expected y ≈ 26.9; A1 states difference large compared with scatter of other points (< 0.4)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three features of a well-drawn graph for these data.
parts.answer: Any three of: axes labelled with quantity and unit; sensible scales using more than half the grid in each direction; points plotted accurately as small crosses; a thin best-fit straight line with points balanced either side; anomalous point identified and not used.

practice.stem: A student loads a spring with mass m and measures the period T of vertical oscillations. Theory suggests T² = (4π²/k)m + c. The graph of T² (s²) against m (kg) has gradient 0.162 s² kg⁻¹ and y-intercept 0.018 s².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the gradient to determine the spring constant k.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the y-intercept of 0.018 s² represents physically.
parts.answer: The effect of the mass of the spring (and hanger) itself, which also oscillates.

practice.stem: A student releases a ball from rest at height h on a ramp and times how long it takes to roll to the bottom, using a hand-held stopwatch. She takes readings at two heights only, one of each, to test whether time t ∝ 1/√h. The times are about 1 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify four sources of uncertainty or limitations of the procedure.
parts.answer: Any four of: (1) only two readings, not enough to draw a valid conclusion; (2) difficult to start the stopwatch exactly as the ball is released and stop it as it reaches the end – reaction time is large compared with short times; (3) difficult to release the ball without pushing it; (4) ball may not roll in a straight line / hits sides; (5) difficult to measure height h to the centre of the ball because of parallax; (6) ramp may bend/surface uneven.
parts.working: B1 each, any four – each must state the quantity affected and the reason

practice.stem: In an experiment with a pendulum, a student ties the string round a rod, times one oscillation by eye with a stopwatch at two different lengths, and measures the length to the bottom of the bob.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest four improvements to the experiment, each linked to a specific problem.
parts.answer: Any four of: (1) take more readings at different lengths and plot a graph; (2) time 20 oscillations / use a light gate and timer, because reaction time is large compared with one period; (3) use a fiducial marker at the centre of the swing to judge complete oscillations; (4) clamp the string between two wooden blocks so the length is fixed and the pivot does not move; (5) use a set-square to measure the length to the centre of the bob, or video with a scale; (6) use small angular amplitude measured with a protractor.
parts.working: B1 each, any four – credit requires a specific method, not 'repeat readings' or 'view at eye level'

practice.stem: A student's best-fit line passes through the points (0.150, 0.92) and (0.650, 2.47), read from a large triangle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the line.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the y-intercept.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the gradient triangle should be large.
parts.answer: To reduce the percentage uncertainty in reading the coordinates.

practice.stem: A student measures the height h of a ball above the bench as 23.5 cm with an absolute uncertainty of 0.2 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in h.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the student gives an uncertainty of 0.2 cm, larger than the smallest division of the rule.
parts.answer: It is difficult to judge the level of the top of the curved surface/ball (parallax, rule held away from object).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student calculates a quantity from h and a time of 1.8 s. State the number of significant figures to which the result should be given, and explain why.
parts.answer: 2 s.f., the same as the least precise raw data (the time).

practice.stem: A ball rolls down a ramp from height h and leaves the bench horizontally, landing a distance d from the bench. Readings: h = 0.100 m, d = 0.316 m; h = 0.400 m, d = 0.620 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate k = d/h for each set of readings and state whether the results support d ∝ h, using the criterion that the two values of k should differ by less than 10 % (difference ÷ smaller value).
parts.answer: k₁ = 3.16, k₂ = 1.55; they differ by about 100 %, so d ∝ h is not supported
parts.working: k₁ = 0.316/0.100 = 3.16, k₂ = 0.620/0.400 = 1.55 (B1); differ by far more than 10 % so not supported (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate K = d/√h for each set of readings and comment on the suggestion that d ∝ √h.
parts.answer: K₁ = 0.999 m¹ᐟ², K₂ = 0.980 m¹ᐟ²; difference 1.9 % < 10 %, so d ∝ √h is supported
