practice.stem: Ripples on the surface of a fish pond in Faisalabad have a frequency of 2.5 Hz and a wavelength of 0.84 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the frequency of a wave.
parts.answer: The number of oscillations (wavelengths passing a point) per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the definitions of speed, frequency and wavelength to show that v = fλ.
parts.answer: In one period T the wave travels one wavelength λ, so v = λ/T, and f = 1/T gives v = fλ.
parts.working: M1 distance λ in time T; A1 f = 1/T leading to v = fλ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the waves and their period.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two points on a progressive wave of wavelength 1.20 m are 0.30 m apart along the direction of travel. What is the phase difference between the oscillations of the two points?
A 45°
B 90°
C 180°
D 270°
parts.working: Phase difference = (0.30/1.20) × 360° = 90°. 180° would need a separation of half a wavelength (0.60 m).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a progressive wave.
parts.answer: A wave that transfers energy from one place to another (without transferring matter).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Explain the meaning of
(i) displacement, (ii) amplitude, (iii) phase difference.
parts.answer: (i) distance (in a given direction) of a point from its equilibrium position; (ii) maximum displacement; (iii) the fraction of a cycle (in degrees or radians) by which one oscillation leads or lags another.

practice.stem: A microphone connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) detects a sound wave. The time-base is set at 2.0 ms per division and the Y-gain at 0.50 V per division. One complete cycle of the trace occupies 4.0 horizontal divisions and the vertical distance from a crest to a trough is 5.2 divisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the frequency of the sound.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the amplitude of the signal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. Calculate the wavelength of the sound.

practice.stem: As a water wave spreads out from a boat on Keenjhar Lake its amplitude falls from 4.0 mm to 2.8 mm. The intensity at the first point is 0.80 W m⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relationship between the intensity and the amplitude of a wave.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity of the wave at the second point.

practice.stem: A transverse wave of frequency 15 Hz travels along a long rope at a speed of 6.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the wave.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Point X on the rope is 0.10 m from point Y and point Z is 0.20 m from Y, all along the direction of travel. Calculate the phase difference, in radians, between
(i) X and Y, (ii) Z and Y.

parts.label: c
parts.text: At one instant Y is at a crest. Describe the displacement and motion of Z at that instant.
parts.answer: Z is at a trough (maximum negative displacement) and momentarily at rest.
parts.working: B1 trough/maximum displacement in opposite direction; B1 instantaneously at rest

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The amplitude of a sound wave increases by 50 %. By what factor does its intensity increase?
A 1.5
B 2.25
C 3.0
D 4.5
parts.working: I ∝ A², so the factor is 1.5² = 2.25. 1.5 assumes intensity is proportional to amplitude.

practice.stem: A small loudspeaker at an open-air event emits sound of power 0.60 W uniformly in all directions. Assume no energy is absorbed by the air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define intensity.
parts.answer: Power transmitted per unit area (perpendicular to the direction of travel).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity of the sound at a distance of 5.0 m from the loudspeaker.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the distance from the loudspeaker at which the amplitude of the sound wave is half its value at 5.0 m.
parts.working: amplitude halved → intensity ÷ 4 (C1); I ∝ 1/r² so r doubles to 10 m (A1)

practice.stem: Two microphones A and B lie on a straight line from a loudspeaker, with B further from the speaker than A. Their signals are shown on a two-trace CRO with time-base 0.50 ms per division. One cycle of each trace occupies 6.0 divisions and the trace from B is shifted 1.5 divisions to the right (lagging) relative to that from A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the sound.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the phase difference between the two signals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Microphone B is moved slowly further from the source along the line from the source. Calculate the extra distance it must be moved, from its original position, before the two traces are next in phase. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: λ = 340/333 = 1.02 m (C1); B lags by ¼ cycle, so it must move a further ¾λ to lag by a whole cycle (C1); 0.75 × 1.02 = 0.765 ≈ 0.77 m (A1)

practice.stem: A hospital ultrasound probe emits waves of frequency 2.5 MHz in short pulses. The speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the ultrasound in the tissue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time between emission of a pulse and detection of its echo from a boundary 6.0 cm below the probe.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each pulse contains 4 complete cycles. Calculate the length of one pulse in the tissue.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of wave cannot be polarised?
A light
B microwaves
C sound in air
D radio waves
parts.working: Only transverse waves can be polarised. Sound in air is longitudinal; the other three are electromagnetic (transverse) waves.

practice.stem: Unpolarised light of intensity 64 W m⁻² is incident on two polarising filters, one after the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the intensity of the light after it has passed through the first polariser.
parts.working: Unpolarised light: half transmitted, 64/2 = 32 W m⁻² (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The transmission axis of the second polariser is at 30° to that of the first. Calculate the intensity of the light leaving the second polariser.
parts.working: I = I₀ cos²θ = 32 cos² 30° (C1) = 24 W m⁻² (A1)

practice.stem: A beam of plane-polarised laser light passes through a polarising filter that can be rotated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Malus's law.
parts.answer: The transmitted intensity I = I₀ cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the plane of polarisation of the light and the transmission axis of the filter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the smallest angle through which the filter must be rotated from the position of maximum transmission so that the transmitted intensity is 20 % of the maximum.

practice.stem: A microwave transmitter emits plane-polarised microwaves towards a receiver connected to a meter. With the receiver aligned with the transmitter, the reading is 0.80 mA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assume the meter reading is proportional to the intensity received. Calculate the reading when the receiver is rotated through 60° about the beam axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the reading is zero when the receiver has been rotated through 90°.
parts.answer: The microwaves are plane-polarised; at 90° the receiver's axis is perpendicular to the plane of oscillation, so no component of the electric field oscillation is detected.
parts.working: B1 transmitter emits plane-polarised waves; B1 cos 90° = 0 / no component along receiver axis

practice.stem: Unpolarised light of intensity 40 W m⁻² passes through polariser 1 and then polariser 3, whose transmission axis is at 90° to that of polariser 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that no light emerges from the arrangement when only polarisers 1 and 3 are present.
parts.answer: Their axes are at 90°, so I = I₁ cos² 90° = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Polariser 2 is now placed between them with its axis at 45° to both. Calculate the intensity of the light that emerges from polariser 3.
parts.working: after 1: 40/2 = 20 W m⁻² (C1); after 2: 20 cos² 45° = 10 W m⁻² (C1); after 3: 10 cos² 45° = 5.0 W m⁻² (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why inserting a filter, which absorbs light, increases the amount of light emerging.
parts.answer: Polariser 2 transmits a component of the light polarised at 45°; this light now has a component along the axis of polariser 3.
parts.working: B1 light leaving 2 polarised at 45°; B1 has non-zero component along axis of 3

practice.stem: Plane-polarised light of intensity 12.0 W m⁻² falls on a polarising filter. The angle between the plane of polarisation and the transmission axis of the filter is θ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by plane-polarised light.
parts.answer: Light in which the oscillations (of the electric field) occur in one plane only, which contains the direction of travel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the transmitted intensity when θ is (i) 20° and (ii) 70°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why polarisation provides evidence that light is a transverse wave.
parts.answer: Only transverse waves have oscillations perpendicular to the direction of travel that can be restricted to one plane.

practice.stem: An ambulance travels at 25 m s⁻¹ along a straight road in Rawalpindi. Its siren emits sound of frequency 950 Hz. A man stands at the roadside. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency heard by the man as the ambulance approaches.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency he hears after it has passed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of wavefronts, why a stationary observer hears a higher frequency when a sound source moves towards him.
parts.answer: The source moves towards the observer between emitting successive wavefronts, so the wavefronts in front are closer together; the wavelength is shorter and, with the same wave speed, more wavefronts arrive per second.
parts.working: B1 wavefronts bunched/shorter wavelength; B1 same speed so higher frequency received

parts.label: b
parts.text: A police car with a 700 Hz siren approaches at 30 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency heard.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A source emitting sound of frequency 500 Hz moves directly away from a stationary observer, who hears a frequency of 480 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the speed of the source?
A 13.6 m s⁻¹
B 14.2 m s⁻¹
C 20.0 m s⁻¹
D 34.0 m s⁻¹
parts.working: 480 = 500 × 340/(340 + v_s) → 340 + v_s = 354.2 → v_s = 14.2 m s⁻¹. 13.6 m s⁻¹ uses 340 × (20/500), the formula for a moving observer.

practice.stem: A girl on a station platform hears the horn of a train passing at constant speed without stopping. The frequency she hears is 560 Hz as the train approaches and 480 Hz as it moves away. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the speed of the train is about 26 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency emitted by the horn.

practice.stem: A small loudspeaker emitting a 1200 Hz note is attached to the end of a rod and moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.80 m at 2.5 revolutions per second. A student stands far away in the plane of the circle. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the loudspeaker.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum and minimum frequencies heard by the student.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the position of the loudspeaker when the student hears the frequency 1200 Hz. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: When it is moving perpendicular to the line to the student (nearest and furthest points of the circle), there is no velocity component towards or away from her.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which list places the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing wavelength?
A γ-rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves
B radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, γ-rays
C γ-rays, ultraviolet, X-rays, visible, microwaves, infrared, radio waves
D X-rays, γ-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, radio waves, microwaves
parts.answer: A γ-rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves
parts.working: γ-rays have the shortest wavelength and radio waves the longest. B is the same list in order of decreasing wavelength.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the approximate range of wavelengths of visible light in a vacuum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of orange light of wavelength 600 nm in a vacuum.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the region of the spectrum for a wavelength of (i) 3 cm, (ii) 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum.
parts.answer: Any two: same speed 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; transverse; can be polarised; travel through a vacuum; consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for a radio signal to travel from the Earth to the Moon, a distance of 3.84 × 10⁸ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An electromagnetic wave has a frequency of 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz. In which region of the spectrum is it?
A radio waves
B microwaves
C infrared
D ultraviolet
parts.working: λ = 3.0 × 10⁸/1.0 × 10¹⁰ = 0.030 m = 3 cm, which is in the microwave region. Radio waves have wavelengths longer than about 0.1–1 m.

practice.stem: A home router in Karachi transmits Wi-Fi signals at 2.4 GHz, and a local FM radio station broadcasts at 101 MHz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of (i) the Wi-Fi signal, (ii) the FM radio signal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A navigation satellite is 2.02 × 10⁷ m above a receiver. Calculate the time for its signal to reach the receiver.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A timing error of 1.0 µs is made in measuring this travel time. Calculate the resulting error in the calculated distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.
parts.answer: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of each type of wave.
parts.answer: Transverse: light / any EM wave / waves on a string. Longitudinal: sound / ultrasound / P-waves.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which wave do the particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction in which the wave transfers energy?
A light from a lamp
B a ripple on water
C sound in air
D a wave on a guitar string
parts.working: Sound in air is longitudinal. A guitar-string wave is transverse: the string moves perpendicular to the wave direction.

practice.stem: One end of a long stretched slinky spring is pushed and pulled along its length at 2.5 Hz. The distance between the centres of two adjacent compressions is 0.72 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a compression and a rarefaction.
parts.answer: Compression: region where the coils (particles) are closer together than normal; rarefaction: region where they are further apart than normal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the wave.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the distance between a compression and the nearest rarefaction.

practice.stem: An earthquake produces longitudinal P-waves travelling at 6.0 km s⁻¹ and transverse S-waves travelling at 3.5 km s⁻¹ through rock. A seismic station in Quetta records the S-waves arriving 24 s after the P-waves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance from the earthquake to the station.

parts.label: b
parts.text: S-waves do not pass through the Earth's liquid outer core. Suggest why.
parts.answer: S-waves are transverse; a liquid cannot support the sideways (shear) forces needed for transverse waves.

practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define electric potential at a point.
parts.answer: The work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point.
parts.working: B1 work done per unit positive charge; B1 from infinity

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential 0.30 m from a point charge of +5.0 nC.

practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an equipotential surface.
parts.answer: A surface on which every point has the same electric potential.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the angle between field lines and equipotential surfaces, and explain why no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.
parts.answer: 90°; there is no potential difference between points on it, so W = qΔV = 0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference between two points at 0.10 m and 0.20 m from a point charge of +4.0 nC.

practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the electric potential near an isolated negative charge is negative.
parts.answer: Potential is zero at infinity; a positive test charge is attracted, so work is done by the field (negative work done on it) as it is brought in from infinity.
parts.working: B1 zero at infinity; B1 attraction → work done on charge is negative

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential energy of an electron and a proton separated by 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

practice.stem: An isolated metal sphere of radius 0.10 m carries a charge of +8.0 nC. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the potential at the surface of the sphere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the potential at a point 0.40 m from the centre of the sphere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the work done in moving a charge of +2.0 nC from the point 0.40 m from the centre to the surface of the sphere.

practice.stem: An alpha particle with kinetic energy 5.0 MeV travels directly towards a gold nucleus. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the alpha particle slows down as it approaches the nucleus.
parts.answer: It is repelled by the positive nucleus; its kinetic energy is converted to electric potential energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance of closest approach. The charge of the gold nucleus is +79e and of the alpha particle +2e. Treat the nucleus as fixed.

practice.stem: The electric potential is 900 V at a distance of 0.20 m from a point charge and 600 V at 0.30 m from it. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the data are consistent with a point charge, and calculate the charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the relationship between field strength and potential gradient to calculate the field strength at 0.20 m from the charge.

practice.stem: An electron starts from rest at a point where the electric potential is −200 V and moves, under electric forces only, to a point where the potential is +300 V. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gain in kinetic energy of the electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate its final speed.

practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one similarity and one difference between gravitational potential near a mass and electric potential near a positive point charge.
parts.answer: Similarity: both ∝ 1/r and both zero at infinity. Difference: gravitational potential is always negative; potential near a positive charge is positive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the work done in bringing a charge of +1.5 µC from infinity to a point 0.25 m from a fixed point charge of +40 nC.

practice.stem: Two small spheres, each of mass 2.0 g and charge +3.0 µC, are held 0.10 m apart. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential energy of the system at the start.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The spheres are released from rest and move apart along a frictionless horizontal track. Calculate the speed of each sphere when they are very far apart.
parts.working: by symmetry each gets half the energy: 0.405 J (C1); ½ × 0.0020 × v² = 0.405 (C1); v = 20 m s⁻¹ (A1)

practice.stem: A point charge of +4.0 nC is fixed at A and a point charge of −1.0 nC is fixed at B, 0.30 m from A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance from A of the point between A and B where the electric potential is zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the electric field strength at this point is not zero.
parts.answer: E is the (negative) potential gradient, not the potential; between opposite charges the fields of both point in the same direction (from A towards B), so they add.
parts.working: B1 E = −dV/dx / V = 0 does not mean gradient zero; B1 fields in same direction

practice.stem: An isolated conducting sphere of radius 0.050 m carries a charge of +6.0 nC in a vacuum. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential at the surface of the sphere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A proton is released from rest at the surface. Calculate its speed when it is very far from the sphere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the proton's acceleration decreases as it moves away.
parts.answer: The field strength (force) decreases with distance as 1/r².

practice.stem: A hollow metal sphere of radius 0.12 m is charged so that the potential at its surface is 6000 V. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the sphere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength just outside the surface.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the electric potential and the field strength at the centre of the sphere.
parts.working: B1 V same as surface (6000 V); B1 E = 0 inside a conductor

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the potential at 0.30 m from the centre.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: Two small charged spheres, of charges +3.0 nC and −5.0 nC, are held with their centres 4.0 cm apart in air. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Coulomb's law.
parts.answer: The force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.
parts.working: B1 ∝ product of charges; B1 ∝ 1/separation² (point charges)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the force between the charges and state whether it is attractive or repulsive.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: An isolated point charge of +12 nC is in a vacuum. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define electric field strength.
parts.answer: Force per unit positive charge (acting on a small stationary charge).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength at a point 0.25 m from the charge.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the force on an electron at this point and state its direction.
parts.working: F = eE = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.73 × 10³ = 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ N (B1); towards the positive charge (B1)

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern of electric field lines around an isolated positive point charge.
parts.answer: Straight radial lines, pointing outwards from the charge, getting further apart with distance.
parts.working: B1 radial/straight lines outwards; B1 spacing increases with distance

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the field lines show where the field is strongest.
parts.answer: The field is strongest where the lines are closest together (near the charge).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The field strength at a distance r from the charge is E. Calculate the field strength at distance 3r, in terms of E.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: A thundercloud model treats a region of charge as a point charge of −6.0 µC. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength 2.0 m from the charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the field at this point.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: The spherical metal dome of a Van de Graaff generator in a school science club has radius 0.15 m. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the charge on the sphere may be treated as a point charge at its centre for points outside the sphere.
parts.answer: The charge is distributed uniformly over the surface (by symmetry), so outside the sphere the field is the same as for a point charge at the centre.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Air breaks down when the field strength exceeds 3.0 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹. Calculate the maximum charge the dome can hold.

parts.label: c
parts.text: With this maximum charge, calculate the field strength at a distance of 0.45 m from the centre of the dome.
parts.working: r is 3 times larger, E ∝ 1/r² (C1); E = 3.0 × 10⁶/9 = 3.3 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ (A1)

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: A point charge of +4.0 µC is fixed at point A and a point charge of +1.0 µC is fixed at point B, 0.30 m from A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is a point between the charges where the electric field strength is zero.
parts.answer: Both charges are positive, so their fields point in opposite directions between them and can cancel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance of this point from A.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the ratio (electric force)/(gravitational force) between two protons is independent of their separation.
parts.answer: Both forces are proportional to 1/r², so r cancels in the ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this ratio. The gravitational constant G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why gravitational forces, not electric forces, dominate the motion of planets.
parts.answer: Planets are electrically neutral overall, so the net electric force is negligible, but mass is always positive so gravity always attracts.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: Two identical small conducting spheres, each of mass 0.20 g, hang from the same point on insulating threads. They are given equal charges and come to rest with each thread at 10° to the vertical. The distance between the centres of the spheres is then 5.0 cm. g = 9.81 m s⁻². Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the electric force between the spheres is about 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge on each sphere.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: Point charges of +2.0 nC and −2.0 nC are fixed at points A and B respectively, 0.10 m apart in a vacuum. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength at the midpoint M of AB and state its direction.
parts.working: each field = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.050² = 7.19 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (C1); both point from A towards B, so they add (C1); 1.44 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ towards B (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Point P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, 0.12 m from M. Determine the electric field strength at P.
parts.answer: 8.2 × 10² N C⁻¹, parallel to AB, towards B
parts.working: AP = BP = 0.13 m; each field = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.13² = 1.06 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (C1); perpendicular components cancel, parallel components add: 2 × 1.06 × 10³ × (0.050/0.13) (C1) = 8.2 × 10² N C⁻¹ parallel to AB towards B (A1)

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, an electron moves in a circular orbit of radius 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m around a proton. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric force on the electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: This force provides the centripetal force. Calculate the speed of the electron.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem:
A probe measures the electric field strength E at distances r from the centre of a charged metal sphere.
r / m: 0.20, 0.30, 0.40
E / 10⁴ V m⁻¹: 4.50, 2.00, 1.125
Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the data are consistent with the field of a point charge at the centre of the sphere.
parts.answer: Er² = 1800 V m in each case, so E ∝ 1/r².
parts.working: M1 calculates Er² (or ratio) for all three; A1 constant 1.80 × 10³ V m so inverse-square

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the charge on the sphere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the distance from the centre at which the field strength would be 5.0 × 10³ V m⁻¹.

practice.stem: Two parallel horizontal metal plates are 4.0 cm apart. The potential difference between them is 600 V. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the force on an oil drop carrying a charge of +3e between the plates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the electric field between two parallel charged plates, away from the edges.
parts.answer: Uniform: field lines parallel, equally spaced, perpendicular to the plates, from positive to negative plate.
parts.working: B1 parallel/equally spaced (uniform); B1 perpendicular to plates, + to −

parts.label: b
parts.text: The plates are 2.5 mm apart in an air-filled capacitor with a p.d. of 9.0 V. Calculate the field strength.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the force on a charged particle varies as it moves from one plate to the other.

practice.stem: An oil drop of mass 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary between two horizontal plates 6.0 mm apart when the potential difference between them is 294 V. g = 9.81 m s⁻². Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the direction of the electric force on the drop and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Upwards, to balance its weight (resultant force zero).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the drop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the number of excess electrons or missing electrons on the drop, and state which it is if the upper plate is positive.
parts.working: 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3 (B1); force upward towards positive plate, so negative: 3 excess electrons (B1)

practice.stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 250 V in an electron gun. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy gained by the electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final speed of the electron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on the final speed of doubling the accelerating potential difference.
parts.answer: Speed increases by a factor of √2.

practice.stem: In an electrostatic dust collector in a cement factory chimney, two vertical parallel plates 0.20 m apart have a potential difference of 40 kV between them. A dust particle of mass 1.0 × 10⁻¹² kg carries a charge of 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the dust particle, ignoring gravity and air resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The particle starts from rest midway between the plates. Calculate the time it takes to reach a plate.

practice.stem: An electron moving horizontally at 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ enters the uniform field between two horizontal parallel plates midway between them. The plates are 5.0 cm long and 2.0 cm apart, with a potential difference of 150 V between them. Ignore gravity. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the electron between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time the electron spends between the plates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the vertical deflection of the electron as it leaves the plates, and state whether it hits a plate.
parts.answer: 4.1 mm; it does not hit a plate (it is 10 mm from each plate)
parts.working: y = ½at² = ½ × 1.32 × 10¹⁵ × (2.5 × 10⁻⁹)² = 4.1 × 10⁻³ m (C1); 4.1 mm < 10 mm so it emerges (A1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the shape of the path of the electron between the plates.
parts.answer: A parabola (constant horizontal velocity, constant vertical acceleration).

practice.stem: A proton and an alpha particle, both initially at rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the speed of a charged particle accelerated from rest through a p.d. V is v = √(2qV/m).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (speed of proton)/(speed of alpha particle). Take the alpha particle mass as 4mₚ and charge 2e.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (kinetic energy of proton)/(kinetic energy of alpha particle).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define simple harmonic motion.
parts.answer: Motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and is always directed towards that point (opposite to the displacement).
parts.working: B1 a ∝ x; B1 directed towards the fixed point / opposite to x

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the defining equation of simple harmonic motion and state the meaning of each symbol.
parts.answer: a = −ω²x; a acceleration, ω angular frequency, x displacement from equilibrium.

practice.stem: A mass hanging from a spring oscillates vertically. A student measures the time for 20 complete oscillations as 13.6 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period of the oscillations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angular frequency.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the student times 20 oscillations rather than one.
parts.answer: To reduce the percentage uncertainty in the period (reaction time is a smaller fraction of the total time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define (i) the period and (ii) the angular frequency of an oscillation.
parts.answer: (i) the time for one complete oscillation; (ii) 2π × frequency (rate of change of phase angle), ω = 2π/T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mains supply in Pakistan has a frequency of 50 Hz. Calculate its period and its angular frequency.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each motion, state whether it is simple harmonic and give a reason.
(i) a ball bouncing vertically on a hard floor
(ii) a mass oscillating on a vertical spring
(iii) a child on a swing with small amplitude
parts.answer: (i) not SHM – acceleration is constant (g) during flight, not proportional to displacement; (ii) SHM – restoring force ∝ displacement; (iii) approximately SHM for small angles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the condition needed for a simple pendulum to move with approximately simple harmonic motion.

practice.stem: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion of angular frequency 15 rad s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the particle when its displacement is +2.0 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the oscillation.

practice.stem: The needle of a sewing machine moves up and down with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 3.0 cm and frequency 2.0 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the needle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration of the needle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where in its motion the needle has its maximum acceleration.
parts.answer: At the extremes of its motion (maximum displacement).

practice.stem: A trolley held between two springs oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 5.0 cm and angular frequency 8.0 rad s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the trolley.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the trolley when its displacement is 3.0 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of its acceleration at this displacement.

practice.stem: A block of mass 0.40 kg oscillates with simple harmonic motion of angular frequency 6.0 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 5.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy of the oscillations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy and the potential energy when the displacement is 3.0 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the kinetic energy varies with displacement x, and state the shape of the graph of kinetic energy against x.
parts.answer: KE is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±x₀; the graph is an inverted parabola.
parts.working: B1 max at centre, zero at ends; B1 inverted parabola

practice.stem:
A data-logger records the acceleration a of a pendulum bob at different displacements x.
x / cm: −4.0, −2.0, 0, 2.0, 4.0
a / m s⁻²: 1.58, 0.79, 0, −0.79, −1.58

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the data show that the motion is simple harmonic.
parts.answer: a is proportional to x (a/x constant = −39.5 s⁻²) and opposite in sign to x.
parts.working: B1 proportional; B1 opposite sign/directed to equilibrium

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the angular frequency and the period of the oscillation.

practice.stem: Two identical pendulums A and B each have period 2.0 s. B reaches its maximum displacement to the right 0.25 s after A does.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the phase difference between the two pendulums in degrees and in radians.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which pendulum leads.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Pendulum B is adjusted so that it reaches maximum displacement on one side at the same instant as A reaches maximum displacement on the other side. State the new phase difference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the graph of acceleration a against displacement x for an object moving with simple harmonic motion.
parts.answer: A straight line through the origin with negative gradient, extending from −x₀ to +x₀.
parts.working: B1 straight line through origin; B1 negative gradient, between ±x₀

parts.label: b
parts.text: For one oscillator the gradient of this graph is −25 s⁻². Calculate the period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of the graph of velocity against displacement.
parts.answer: An ellipse (a circle if axes are suitably scaled), centred on the origin.

practice.stem: An oscillator moving with simple harmonic motion has total energy 2.4 mJ and amplitude 2.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the potential energy of the oscillator when its displacement is 1.0 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy at this displacement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the displacement at which the kinetic energy equals the potential energy.

practice.stem: Water in a U-tube is displaced and then oscillates. The acceleration a of the water surface is related to its displacement x from equilibrium by a = −(2g/L)x, where L = 0.40 m is the total length of the water column and g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the motion of the liquid is simple harmonic.
parts.answer: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and in the opposite direction (a = −(2g/L)x has the form a = −ω²x).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period of oscillation of the liquid.

practice.stem: A data-logger shows that the velocity of a swinging lantern varies sinusoidally with time, with maximum value 0.60 m s⁻¹ and period 1.5 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amplitude of the oscillation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration.

practice.stem: A buoy in the sea at Gwadar bobs up and down with simple harmonic motion. It makes 12 complete oscillations in 30 s and the vertical distance between its highest and lowest positions is 0.50 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period and the maximum speed of the buoy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the displacement of the buoy 0.40 s after it passes upwards through its equilibrium position.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the phase difference between (i) the velocity and the displacement, (ii) the acceleration and the displacement.
parts.answer: (i) π/2 rad (velocity leads by 90°) (ii) π rad (antiphase)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The maximum speed of an oscillator is 0.80 m s⁻¹. Calculate its speed when the displacement is half the amplitude.

practice.stem: The displacement x of an oscillating object is given by x = 0.12 sin(5.0t), where x is in metres and t is in seconds (angles in radians).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the amplitude and the period of the oscillation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the displacement and the velocity of the object at t = 0.40 s.
parts.working: x = 0.12 sin(2.0 rad) = 0.109 m (B1); v = 0.12 × 5.0 cos(2.0 rad) (C1) = −0.25 m s⁻¹, i.e. moving back towards equilibrium (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the first time after t = 0 at which the displacement is 0.060 m.

practice.stem: The piston of a car engine moves with approximately simple harmonic motion. The total distance moved between its highest and lowest positions (the stroke) is 9.0 cm. The engine turns at 3000 revolutions per minute, with one oscillation of the piston per revolution. The mass of the piston is 0.35 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular frequency of the piston's motion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration of the piston.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum resultant force on the piston.

practice.stem: At a harbour near Karachi the height of the sea above its mean level varies approximately with simple harmonic motion, with amplitude 1.8 m and period 12.4 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the height h of the water above mean level at time t, taking h = +1.8 m (high tide) at t = 0.
parts.working: B1 cos form with amplitude 1.8; B1 ω = 2π/12.4 = 0.507 rad h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: A ship can only pass the harbour entrance when the water is at least 1.0 m above mean level. Calculate the length of time in each tidal cycle during which the ship can pass.
parts.working: 1.8 cos ωt = 1.0 → ωt = 0.982 rad (C1); time from 0.982/0.507 = 1.94 h before to 1.94 h after high tide (C1); window = 3.9 h (A1)

practice.stem: A trolley of mass 0.25 kg on a horizontal frictionless track is attached to a spring system that provides a restoring force F = −kx, where k = 40 N m⁻¹ and x is the displacement. The trolley is pulled 4.0 cm from equilibrium and released.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By considering the resultant force, show that the trolley moves with simple harmonic motion and that ω = √(k/m).
parts.answer: F = −kx so a = −(k/m)x, which has the form a = −ω²x with ω² = k/m.
parts.working: M1 F = −kx and a = F/m; A1 compare with a = −ω²x

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period of the oscillations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed and the maximum kinetic energy of the trolley.

practice.stem: An object moves with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 2.5 cm. At t = 0 it passes through its equilibrium position moving in the positive direction. It first reaches its maximum positive displacement at t = 0.15 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the period and the angular frequency.
parts.working: max displacement reached at a quarter period, so T = 4 × 0.15 = 0.60 s (B1); ω = 2π/0.60 = 10.5 rad s⁻¹ (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the velocity of the object at t = 0.10 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the object at t = 0.10 s.
parts.working: a = −ω²x₀ sin ωt = −10.5² × 0.025 × sin(1.05 rad) (C1) = −2.4 m s⁻² (A1)

practice.stem: A coin rests on a horizontal platform that oscillates vertically with simple harmonic motion of frequency 4.0 Hz. The amplitude is slowly increased. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the coin may lose contact with the platform, and state at which point in the oscillation this first happens.
parts.answer: At the top of the motion the platform's downward acceleration is greatest; if this exceeds g, the coin (whose maximum downward acceleration is g) cannot follow and leaves the surface.
parts.working: B1 needed downward acceleration > g; B1 at the highest point

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum amplitude at which the coin loses contact.

practice.stem: The tip of each prong of a tuning fork vibrates with simple harmonic motion of frequency 440 Hz and amplitude 0.50 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the tip of the prong.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration of the tip and express it as a multiple of g (9.81 m s⁻²).

practice.stem: When four passengers of total mass 300 kg get into a car, the car body moves down by 4.9 cm. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effective spring constant of the suspension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The loaded car (total mass 1500 kg) bounces vertically after going over a bump. Assuming the motion is simple harmonic with ω = √(k/m), calculate the period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the period of the passengers leaving the car.
parts.answer: The period decreases because the mass decreases (T ∝ √m).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by damping.
parts.answer: The loss of energy (and so a decrease in amplitude) of an oscillating system caused by resistive forces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the motion of a system that is (i) lightly damped, (ii) critically damped, (iii) heavily damped, after being displaced and released.
parts.answer: (i) oscillates with amplitude decreasing gradually (period nearly unchanged); (ii) returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating; (iii) returns to equilibrium slowly without oscillating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which type of damping is used in the suspension of a car and explain why.
parts.answer: Critical damping, so the car returns to its rest position quickly without bouncing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by resonance.
parts.answer: When the driving frequency of a forced oscillation equals the natural frequency of the system, the amplitude is a maximum (maximum energy transfer).
parts.working: B1 driving frequency = natural frequency; B1 maximum amplitude

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of increasing the damping on the graph of amplitude against driving frequency.
parts.answer: The peak amplitude is lower at all frequencies, the peak becomes broader (flatter), and the resonant frequency shifts slightly lower.
parts.working: B1 lower amplitude; B1 broader peak; B1 peak moves to lower frequency

practice.stem: A lightly damped pendulum is released with amplitude 10.0 cm. After 5 complete oscillations its amplitude is 8.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the original energy that remains after 5 oscillations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume the amplitude decreases by the same fraction in every 5 oscillations. Calculate the amplitude after 10 oscillations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one cause of the damping.
parts.answer: Air resistance (or friction at the pivot).

practice.stem:
A mass on a spring is driven by a vibration generator. The amplitude A of the forced oscillations is measured at different driving frequencies f.
f / Hz: 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0
A / cm: 0.8, 1.6, 4.9, 1.9, 0.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the natural frequency of the system and explain how you identified it.
parts.answer: About 2.0 Hz, where the amplitude is a maximum (resonance).
parts.working: B1 2.0 Hz; B1 maximum amplitude at resonance

parts.label: b
parts.text: The oscillating mass is 0.30 kg. Using ω² = k/m, estimate the spring constant of the spring.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mass is replaced by one of 1.20 kg. State the new natural frequency.

practice.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg has a suspension of effective spring constant 6.0 × 10⁴ N m⁻¹. It drives over a series of speed bumps spaced 9.0 m apart along a road in Islamabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the natural frequency of vertical oscillation of the car on its suspension, using f = (1/2π)√(k/m).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which the car would bounce with the largest amplitude, and explain your answer.
parts.working: bumps act as a periodic driving force (B1); resonance when bump frequency v/9.0 = 1.13 Hz (C1); v = 10 m s⁻¹ (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the shock absorbers are designed to give a large amount of damping (close to critical damping).
parts.answer: The damping reduces the amplitude at resonance and makes the car return to its rest position quickly, without continuing to bounce.
parts.working: B1 smaller amplitude at resonance / oscillations die away quickly

practice.stem: A footbridge across a canal has a natural frequency of vertical oscillation of 2.0 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A group of joggers, each with a stride of 1.5 m, crosses the bridge in step. Calculate the jogging speed at which the bridge would oscillate with the largest amplitude.
parts.working: resonance when step frequency = 2.0 Hz (C1); v = 2.0 × 1.5 = 3.0 m s⁻¹ (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why soldiers are often told to break step when marching across a bridge.
parts.answer: Marching in step gives a periodic driving force; if its frequency matches the natural frequency of the bridge, resonance causes large, possibly damaging, oscillations.
parts.working: B1 periodic force at one frequency; B1 resonance → large amplitude

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way engineers can reduce the risk without changing the bridge's natural frequency.
parts.answer: Fit dampers (e.g. tuned mass dampers or viscous dampers) to increase damping.

practice.stem: Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of neutron = 1.008665 u; mass of ⁴₂He nucleus = 4.001506 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define mass defect of a nucleus.
parts.answer: The difference between the total mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass defect of a helium-4 nucleus in u.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of helium-4 in MeV.

practice.stem: Speed of light c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the equation that relates energy to mass, explaining each symbol.
parts.answer: E = mc², where E is energy, m is mass and c is the speed of light in a vacuum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy equivalent of 1.0 g of mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Sun radiates energy at a rate of 3.85 × 10²⁶ W. Calculate the mass the Sun loses each second because of this.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the general shape of a graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number A.
parts.answer: Rises steeply from very low values for the lightest nuclei (with ⁴He a local peak); reaches a broad maximum of about 8.8 MeV near A ≈ 56–62 (iron/nickel); then decreases slowly to about 7.6 MeV for the heaviest nuclei.
parts.working: B1 steep rise for small A; B1 maximum ≈ 8.8 MeV around A ≈ 56 (Fe); B1 gradual decrease for large A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the shape of the graph to explain why both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy.
parts.answer: In both cases the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the original nuclei (they move towards the peak), so the total binding energy increases and the mass decreases; the mass difference is released as energy.
parts.working: B1 products have greater BE per nucleon (closer to peak); B1 increase in total BE / decrease in mass released as energy.

practice.stem: A deuteron (²₁H nucleus) has a mass of 2.013553 u. Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of neutron = 1.008665 u.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that 1 u is equivalent to about 934 MeV using u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy of the deuteron in joules, using u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express this binding energy in MeV.

practice.stem: A possible fission reaction is ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n. The total mass of the products is 0.186 u less than the total mass of the reactants. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the value of x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in one fission, in MeV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the neutrons produced can lead to a chain reaction, and why a moderator is needed in a reactor.
parts.answer: Each fission releases more than one neutron, and each can cause a further fission; a moderator slows the fast neutrons down so they are more likely to be absorbed by U-235 and cause fission.
parts.working: B1 neutrons released go on to cause further fissions; B1 moderator slows neutrons (thermal neutrons more likely to cause fission).

practice.stem: The nucleus ⁵⁶₂₆Fe has a mass of 55.920662 u. Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of neutron = 1.008665 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy of an iron-56 nucleus in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why iron-56 cannot release energy by either fission or fusion.
parts.answer: It is at (or very near) the peak of the binding energy per nucleon curve; any products of fission or fusion would have lower binding energy per nucleon, so energy would have to be supplied.
parts.working: B1 near maximum BE per nucleon; B1 products would have lower BE/nucleon, so energy absorbed not released.

practice.stem: In a fusion reactor, deuterium and tritium fuse: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n. Masses: ²₁H 2.014102 u; ³₁H 3.016049 u; ⁴₂He 4.002603 u; ¹₀n 1.008665 u. (These are atomic masses; the electron masses cancel.) 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in one reaction, in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why fusion requires a very high temperature.
parts.answer: The nuclei are both positively charged and repel; they need very high kinetic energies (high temperature) to overcome the electrostatic repulsion and get close enough for the strong force to act.
parts.working: B1 electrostatic repulsion between positive nuclei; B1 high KE to approach closely (within range of strong force).

practice.stem: Each fission of a uranium-235 nucleus releases about 200 MeV. Molar mass of U-235 = 0.235 kg mol⁻¹; Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J; 1 day = 86 400 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the energy released by the complete fission of 1.0 kg of uranium-235 is about 8 × 10¹³ J.
parts.working: Number of nuclei = (1.0 ÷ 0.235) × 6.02 × 10²³ = 2.56 × 10²⁴ (M1); energy per fission = 200 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J (M1); total = 8.20 × 10¹³ J (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A power station produces 600 MW of electrical power with an overall efficiency of 33%. Calculate the mass of uranium-235 used each day.
parts.working: Input power = 600 ÷ 0.33 = 1820 MW (C1); energy per day = 1.57 × 10¹⁴ J (M1); mass = 1.92 kg (A1).

practice.stem: Radium-226 decays by α-emission to radon-222. Atomic masses: Ra-226 226.025410 u; Rn-222 222.017578 u; He-4 4.002603 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the nuclear equation for this decay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in the decay, in MeV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the alpha particle carries away most of this energy as kinetic energy.
parts.answer: Momentum is conserved and the radium was at rest, so the α-particle and radon nucleus have equal and opposite momenta; KE = p²/2m, so the much lighter α-particle has much more KE.
parts.working: B1 equal and opposite momenta; B1 KE = p²/2m so lighter particle has greater KE.

practice.stem: Binding energies per nucleon: ²³⁵₉₂U 7.591 MeV; ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba 8.326 MeV; ⁹²₃₆Kr 8.513 MeV. Consider the fission ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3 ¹₀n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the binding energy of the free neutrons does not appear in the calculation.
parts.answer: A free neutron is not bound in a nucleus, so its binding energy is zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total binding energy of each of the three nuclei.
parts.working: BE = A × (BE per nucleon) (M1); three correct values (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the energy released in the fission.

practice.stem: In the fusion reaction ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n, the energy released is 17.6 MeV, shared as kinetic energy between the helium nucleus and the neutron.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assuming the initial momentum is negligible, show that the neutron receives about 4/5 of the energy released.
parts.answer: Equal and opposite momenta p; KE = p²/2m, so KEₙ/KE_α = m_α/mₙ ≈ 4; neutron gets 4/(4 + 1) = 4/5.
parts.working: M1 equal momenta and KE = p²/2m; A1 ratio 4:1 hence 4/5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the neutron in MeV, using the mass ratio m_α/mₙ = 4.002603/1.008665.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the neutron, treating it non-relativistically. (mass of neutron = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the energy of fusion reactors is captured using a blanket of material surrounding the plasma.
parts.answer: The neutrons are uncharged so magnetic fields cannot contain them; they escape the plasma and deposit their kinetic energy (as heat) in the blanket.

practice.stem: In the core of the Sun the net effect of a chain of fusion reactions is 4 ¹₁p → ⁴₂He + 2 ⁰₊₁e + 2ν. Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of ⁴₂He nucleus = 4.001506 u; mass of positron = 0.000549 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in this reaction, in MeV, ignoring the neutrinos' mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the annihilation of the two positrons is included, the total energy released per helium nucleus formed is 26.7 MeV. The Sun's power output is 3.85 × 10²⁶ W. Calculate the number of helium nuclei formed in the Sun each second.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the mass of hydrogen (protons) converted each second. (mass of proton = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)

practice.stem: A D–T fusion reaction (²₁H + ³₁H) releases 17.6 MeV. A fission of U-235 (²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n) releases 200 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per nucleon of reactants for each reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the ratio (energy released per kilogram of fusion fuel) ÷ (energy released per kilogram of fission fuel).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fission reaction still releases much more energy per reaction than the fusion reaction.
parts.answer: Energy released = change in total binding energy; uranium has 236 nucleons, each gaining about 0.85 MeV of binding energy, so the total is large even though the gain per nucleon is small.
parts.working: B1 many more nucleons involved; B1 total = number of nucleons × increase in BE per nucleon.

practice.stem: Binding energies per nucleon: ⁶₃Li 5.33 MeV; ⁴₂He 7.07 MeV; ³₁H 2.83 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in the reaction ⁶₃Li + ¹₀n → ⁴₂He + ³₁H.
parts.working: Total BE: He-4 = 4 × 7.07 = 28.28 MeV; H-3 = 3 × 2.83 = 8.49 MeV; Li-6 = 6 × 5.33 = 31.98 MeV (M1); energy released = BE(products) − BE(reactants) (M1) = 28.28 + 8.49 − 31.98 = 4.79 MeV (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the free neutron contributes nothing to the reactants' binding energy.
parts.answer: It is not part of a nucleus, so it has no binding energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: This reaction is used to make tritium for fusion reactors. Explain why it releases energy even though neither reaction type is 'fission of heavy' or 'fusion of light' nuclei in the usual sense.
parts.answer: Energy is released whenever the products have a greater total binding energy than the reactants; ⁴He has an unusually high binding energy per nucleon, so the total binding energy increases.
parts.working: B1 total BE increases; B1 helium-4 especially tightly bound.

practice.stem: Plutonium-239 decays by α-emission: ²³⁹₉₄Pu → ²³⁵₉₂U + ⁴₂He. Atomic masses: Pu-239 239.052163 u; U-235 235.043930 u; He-4 4.002603 u. Use nucleon numbers for the ratio of masses. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in the decay in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the α-particle carries a fraction 235/239 of this energy, and calculate its kinetic energy.
parts.working: Equal and opposite momenta (M1); KE_α/KE_U = m_U/m_α = 235/4, so KE_α = E × 235/239 (M1); = 5.16 MeV (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the recoiling uranium nucleus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the decay constant of a radioactive nuclide.
parts.answer: The probability per unit time that a nucleus will decay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the relationship between the decay constant λ and the half-life t½.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Iodine-131, used to treat thyroid conditions, has a half-life of 8.02 days. Calculate its decay constant in s⁻¹.

practice.stem: Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.27 years. 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the activity of a radioactive sample.
parts.answer: The number of nuclei decaying per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the decay constant of cobalt-60 in s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activity of a sample containing 2.0 × 10¹² cobalt-60 nuclei.

practice.stem: A hospital in Islamabad prepares a technetium-99m sample for a medical scan. Its initial activity is 800 MBq and its half-life is 6.0 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity of the sample 24 hours after it is prepared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity 9.0 hours after it is prepared.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a short half-life is useful for a tracer injected into a patient.
parts.answer: The activity in the body falls quickly, so the patient receives a smaller total dose of radiation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by radioactive decay being (i) spontaneous and (ii) random.
parts.answer: (i) It is not affected by external conditions such as temperature or pressure; (ii) it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay (each nucleus has a constant probability of decay per unit time).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the evidence for the random nature of decay that can be seen when using a Geiger–Müller counter.
parts.answer: The count rate fluctuates (repeated counts over equal time intervals vary).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A counter records 350 counts in 5.0 minutes near a source. The background count rate is 25 counts per minute. Calculate the corrected count rate due to the source.
parts.working: 350 ÷ 5.0 = 70 counts per minute (M1); 70 − 25 = 45 counts per minute (A1).

practice.stem: Wood from an ancient boat found near the Indus has a carbon-14 activity of 0.115 Bq per gram of carbon. Living wood has an activity of 0.250 Bq per gram of carbon. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that A = A₀e^(−λt) can be rearranged to give t = (t½/ln 2) × ln(A₀/A).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the age of the wood.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in this calculation.
parts.answer: The activity per gram of living wood was the same when the tree died as it is today (atmospheric C-14 level constant) / the sample has not been contaminated.

practice.stem: A sample contains 1.0 µg of strontium-90 (half-life 28.8 years). Unified atomic mass unit u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of strontium-90 nuclei in the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity of the sample.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activity after 50 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starting from dN/dt = −λN, state the expression for the number N of undecayed nuclei after time t, and explain why the activity follows the same law.
parts.answer: N = N₀e^(−λt); A = λN, and λ is constant, so A = A₀e^(−λt).
parts.working: B1 N = N₀e^(−λt); B1 A ∝ N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for the activity of a sodium-24 sample (half-life 15.0 hours) to fall to 10% of its initial value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the time to fall from 100% to 50% is the same as the time to fall from 20% to 10%.
parts.answer: Decay is exponential: the half-life is constant, independent of the amount present.

practice.stem: Fluorine-18, used in PET scanning, has a half-life of 110 minutes. A patient must receive an activity of 400 MBq at the time of injection, 2.5 hours after the dose is prepared in a cyclotron unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity that must be prepared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity remaining in the patient 12 hours after injection, ignoring any loss from the body.

practice.stem:
A student records the count rate C (corrected for background) from a short-lived source.
t / min: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25
C / min⁻¹: 1200, 778, 505, 327, 212, 138
ln (C / min⁻¹): 7.09, 6.66, 6.22, 5.79, 5.36, 4.93

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph of ln C against t should be a straight line, and state what its gradient represents.
parts.answer: C = C₀e^(−λt) gives ln C = ln C₀ − λt (form y = c + mx); gradient = −λ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the first and last values of ln C to find the gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine the half-life of the source.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why it is better to plot ln C against t than to read the half-life directly from a graph of C against t.
parts.answer: A straight-line graph tests the exponential relationship and uses all the data (best-fit line), reducing the effect of random fluctuations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two sources P and Q have the same initial activity. The half-life of P is 2.0 hours and that of Q is 6.0 hours. Calculate the ratio (activity of P) ÷ (activity of Q) after 12 hours.
parts.working: P: 12/2 = 6 half-lives, A = A₀/64 (M1); Q: 2 half-lives, A = A₀/4 (M1); ratio = 4/64 = 1/16 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the ratio (number of undecayed nuclei of P) ÷ (number of undecayed nuclei of Q) at the start.
parts.working: A = λN so N ∝ A/λ ∝ A × t½ (M1); equal A, so N_P/N_Q = 2.0/6.0 = 1/3 (A1).

practice.stem: Uranium-238 decays through a chain of short-lived nuclides to stable lead-206; the overall half-life is 4.47 × 10⁹ years. A rock sample contains 0.30 lead-206 nuclei for every uranium-238 nucleus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the number of uranium-238 nuclei remaining is 1/1.30 of the original number.
parts.working: Each decayed U nucleus gives one Pb nucleus, so N₀ = N_U + N_Pb = N_U(1 + 0.30) (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the age of the rock.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two assumptions made.
parts.answer: No lead-206 was present when the rock formed; no uranium or lead has entered or left the rock (and the intermediate nuclides in the chain are negligible).

practice.stem: A cobalt-60 source (half-life 5.27 years) for a cancer treatment machine must have an initial activity of 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq. u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of cobalt-60 nuclei needed for an activity of 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of cobalt-60 needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The source is replaced when its activity falls below 2.0 × 10¹⁰ Bq. Calculate how long after manufacture this happens.

practice.stem: Air in a basement contains radon-222 (half-life 3.82 days) with an activity of 200 Bq per cubic metre. u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 day = 86 400 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of radon-222 atoms in each cubic metre of air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of radon in each cubic metre of air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The supply of radon from the ground is stopped by sealing the floor. Calculate how many days it takes for the activity to fall to 20 Bq m⁻³, assuming no ventilation.

practice.stem: Polonium-210 (half-life 138 days) emits α-particles of energy 5.30 MeV and has been used as a compact heat source in spacecraft. u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J; 1 day = 86 400 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial activity of 1.0 g of polonium-210.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the initial thermal power produced, assuming all the α-particle energy is absorbed in the capsule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time, in days, for the power to fall to 25 W.
parts.working: P ∝ A, so t = (t½/ln 2) ln(P₀/25) (M1) = 345 days (A1).

practice.stem: A detector placed near a small caesium-137 source (half-life 30.2 years) records a count rate of 480 per minute after correction for background. The detector records only 2.0% of the emissions from the source. u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity of the source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of caesium-137 nuclei in the source.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of caesium-137 in the source.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the detector records only a small fraction of the emissions.
parts.answer: Emissions go in all directions and only a small fraction enter the detector window (and not all that enter are detected).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a photon.
parts.answer: A discrete quantum (packet) of electromagnetic energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A green laser pointer emits light of wavelength 532 nm. Calculate the energy of one photon in joules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express this energy in electronvolts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define work function.
parts.answer: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of the metal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define threshold frequency.
parts.answer: The minimum frequency of electromagnetic radiation that causes electrons to be emitted from the surface.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The work function of zinc is 4.30 eV. Calculate its threshold frequency.
parts.working: C1 φ = hf₀ with φ = 4.30 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; A1 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the momentum of a photon of red light of wavelength 650 nm.
parts.working: C1 p = h/λ; A1 1.02 × 10⁻²⁷ N s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the energy E of a photon is related to its momentum p by E = pc, and use this to find the photon energy.
parts.answer: E = hf = hc/λ = (h/λ)c = pc; E = 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three observations from photoelectric emission experiments that cannot be explained by a wave theory of light.
parts.answer: Any three: no emission below a threshold frequency however intense the light; emission is instantaneous even at low intensity; the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on frequency, not intensity; increasing intensity increases the rate of emission only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the photon model accounts for the existence of a threshold frequency.
parts.answer: Each electron absorbs the energy of one photon, E = hf; if hf is less than the work function no electron can escape, however many photons arrive.
parts.working: B1 one photon to one electron; B1 hf < φ means no emission

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the electronvolt.
parts.answer: The energy gained (transferred) when an electron moves through a potential difference of one volt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 3.5 eV into joules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of a photon of energy 3.5 eV and state the region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
parts.working: B1 λ = hc/E value; B1 ultraviolet

parts.label: a
parts.text: An FM radio station in Islamabad broadcasts at 98.6 MHz. Calculate the energy of one of its photons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why radio waves cannot cause photoelectric emission from a metal, however intense they are.
parts.answer: Each photon's energy is far below any metal's work function (a few eV ≈ 10⁻¹⁹ J), and an electron absorbs only one photon, so no electron gains enough energy.
parts.working: B1 photon energy much less than work function; B1 one photon per electron / intensity only increases number of photons

practice.stem: Ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 250 nm falls on a clean potassium surface. The work function of potassium is 2.30 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy of each photon in eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons in eV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the emitted electrons.
parts.working: C1 ½mv² = 4.28 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; A1 v = 9.69 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why most emitted electrons have less than this kinetic energy.
parts.answer: Electrons below the surface lose energy (in collisions) before escaping, or need more than the work function to escape.

practice.stem:
In a photoelectric experiment, light of different frequencies f falls on a metal surface, and the maximum kinetic energy KE_max of the emitted electrons is measured in electronvolts.
f / 10¹⁴ Hz | KE_max / eV
6.0 | 0.25
7.0 | 0.64
8.0 | 1.06
9.0 | 1.50
10.0 | 1.88

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that a graph of KE_max (in eV) against f should be a straight line, and state expressions for its gradient and its intercept on the KE_max axis.
parts.answer: hf = φ + KE_max, so KE_max = (h/e)f − φ/e with KE in eV; gradient = h/e, intercept = −φ (in eV).
parts.working: B1 rearranged equation; B1 gradient h/e and intercept −φ/e

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the first and last rows (or a best-fit line), determine a value for the Planck constant.
parts.working: M1 gradient (in V s) × e; A1 h in range with unit

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the work function of the metal in eV.
parts.working: M1 φ = hf/e − KE_max for a point on the line (or −intercept); A1 φ

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the threshold frequency.
parts.working: f₀ = φ/h, or the intercept on the f axis: 6.0 × 10¹⁴ − 0.25/(gradient 4.075 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s) (A1, consistent with (b) and (c))

practice.stem: A red laser pointer emits light of wavelength 650 nm with an output power of 5.0 mW.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of photons emitted per second.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second laser of the same power emits blue light of wavelength 450 nm. State and explain whether it emits more or fewer photons per second.
parts.answer: Fewer: each blue photon has more energy (E = hc/λ, smaller λ), so fewer photons are needed for the same power.

practice.stem: A metal with work function 2.20 eV is illuminated with light containing only two wavelengths, 420 nm and 610 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the threshold wavelength for this metal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of the two wavelengths causes photoelectric emission.
parts.answer: 420 nm only (it is shorter than the threshold wavelength; 610 nm is longer).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the emitted electrons.
parts.working: C1 KE_max = hc/λ − φ = 1.22 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; A1 5.17 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Electrons in a dental X-ray tube are accelerated through a p.d. of 25 kV. State the maximum energy of an X-ray photon produced, in keV.
parts.working: An electron can lose all its kinetic energy (25 keV) to one photon (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum wavelength of the X-rays.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the X-rays produced have a continuous range of wavelengths above this minimum.
parts.answer: Electrons lose different amounts of energy in each deceleration (some in several steps), so photons of all energies up to the maximum are produced.

practice.stem: Graphs of the maximum kinetic energy KE_max of photoelectrons against frequency f are plotted for two metals, P and Q. Both are straight lines. The line for P meets the frequency axis at 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz and the line for Q meets it at 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the two lines are parallel.
parts.answer: The gradient of each line equals the Planck constant h (or h/e if KE_max is in eV), which is the same for all metals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the work function of each metal in eV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the intercept that each line would make if extended to the KE_max axis.
parts.answer: −2.28 eV for P and −3.32 eV for Q (minus the work function)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A red LED emits photons of wavelength 630 nm. Each photon is produced when one electron loses energy crossing the junction. Estimate the minimum p.d. needed across the LED.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a blue LED needs a larger p.d. than a red LED.
parts.answer: Blue photons have shorter wavelength and so more energy, so each electron must be given more energy (eV).

practice.stem: Light of wavelength 400 nm and power 2.0 µW falls on the cathode of a photocell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of photons arriving at the cathode per second.
parts.working: C1 E = hc/λ; A1 N = P/E = 4.02 × 10¹² s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: On average, one photon in 500 releases an electron, and all released electrons reach the anode. Calculate the photoelectric current.
parts.working: M1 electrons per second = 8.04 × 10⁹; A1 I = Ne = 1.29 × 10⁻⁹ A

parts.label: c
parts.text: The intensity of the light is doubled at the same wavelength. State the effect on (i) the current and (ii) the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons, and explain.
