parts.answer: (i) current doubles, since twice as many photons arrive per second; (ii) maximum KE unchanged, since each photon's energy hf is unchanged.

practice.stem: Photons carry momentum as well as energy. Solar sails use this to propel spacecraft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the force exerted on a surface that absorbs all the light falling on it is P/c, where P is the power of the light.
parts.answer: Each photon has momentum E/c; the photons arriving per second carry momentum P/c per second; when absorbed, rate of change of momentum = force = P/c.
parts.working: B1 p = E/c per photon; B1 rate of change of momentum = P/c

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the force on a 1.0 m² black panel facing the Sun just outside the Earth's atmosphere, where the intensity is 1.36 kW m⁻².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the force if the panel is replaced by a perfect mirror, and explain the difference.
parts.answer: 9.07 × 10⁻⁶ N; each photon's momentum is reversed, so its change of momentum (and the force) is doubled.

practice.stem: Monochromatic radiation of wavelength 300 nm falls on a metal surface and the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is 1.85 eV. When radiation of wavelength 450 nm is used, the maximum kinetic energy is 0.47 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use these results to determine a value for the Planck constant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the work function of the metal, in eV.
parts.working: C1 φ = hc/λ₁ − KE₁; A1 2.29 eV

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the longest wavelength that will cause emission from this metal.

practice.stem: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 330 nm falls on a metal plate of work function 2.10 eV in a vacuum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the electrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The fastest electrons enter a uniform magnetic field of flux density 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ T at right angles to the field. Calculate the radius of their circular path.
parts.working: C1 Bev = mv²/r, so r = mv/(Be); A1 0.0363 m

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how the paths of slower electrons from the same surface differ.
parts.answer: They move in circles of smaller radius (r ∝ v), in the same sense of rotation.

practice.stem: On a dark night in the Thar desert, a dark-adapted human eye can just detect green light of wavelength 510 nm when 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ W enters the pupil. The pupil diameter is 7.0 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of photons per second entering the eye at this threshold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity at the eye at this threshold.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A lamp radiates 5.0 W of visible light of wavelength 510 nm uniformly in all directions. Estimate the greatest distance at which it could just be seen, ignoring absorption in the air.
parts.working: M1 I = P/(4πd²) set equal to 5.20 × 10⁻¹³ W m⁻²; A1 d = 8.75 × 10⁵ m

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the de Broglie relation, explaining the symbols.
parts.answer: λ = h/p, where λ is the de Broglie wavelength, h the Planck constant and p the momentum of the particle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 2.5 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one phenomenon that provides evidence for the wave nature of electrons and one that provides evidence for the particle nature of electromagnetic radiation.
parts.answer: Electron diffraction (by a thin graphite/crystal film); the photoelectric effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In an electron diffraction tube, the electrons form rings on a fluorescent screen. Explain why this shows wave behaviour.
parts.answer: Rings are a diffraction/interference pattern: maxima and minima form where waves from the atomic layers reinforce or cancel, which particles alone would not produce.
parts.working: B1 diffraction/interference; B1 by the regular atomic spacing comparable with λ

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a p.d. V is λ = h/√(2meV).
parts.answer: eV = ½mv² = p²/2m, so p = √(2meV); λ = h/p = h/√(2meV).
parts.working: B1 KE = eV = p²/2m; B1 substitution

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength for V = 150 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The atomic spacing in a crystal is about 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Explain why electrons of this energy are diffracted significantly by the crystal.
parts.answer: Their wavelength is similar to (the same order as) the atomic spacing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg bowled at 40 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ball shows no observable diffraction when it passes between the stumps.
parts.answer: The wavelength is far smaller than the gap or any obstacle (by more than 30 orders of magnitude), so diffraction is negligible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The accelerating p.d. in an electron diffraction tube is increased from 3.0 kV to 5.0 kV. Calculate the ratio new wavelength ÷ old wavelength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the diameter of the rings on the screen.
parts.answer: The rings become smaller: the shorter wavelength is diffracted through smaller angles.
parts.working: B1 smaller; B1 shorter wavelength, less diffraction

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Show that the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths, λ_electron/λ_proton, equals √(m_p/m_e), and calculate its value.
parts.working: M1 p = √(2mE_k); M1 λ = h/√(2mE_k), so ratio = √(m_p/m_e); A1 42.8

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a proton accelerated from rest through 2.0 kV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a neutron of speed 2200 m s⁻¹ (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate its kinetic energy in eV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why slow neutrons like these are useful for studying the arrangement of atoms in solids.
parts.answer: Their wavelength is about the same as the atomic spacing, so they are diffracted by the crystal lattice (and being uncharged they penetrate the material).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy of a photon of wavelength 0.20 nm, in eV.
parts.working: C1 E = hc/λ = 9.94 × 10⁻¹⁶ J; A1 value in eV

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of an electron with de Broglie wavelength 0.20 nm, in eV.
parts.working: M1 p = h/λ = 3.31 × 10⁻²⁴ N s; M1 E = p²/2m = 6.03 × 10⁻¹⁸ J; A1 value in eV

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why electrons, rather than X-rays, are used to study the structure of thin surface layers.
parts.answer: Electrons of the same wavelength have much less energy, so they penetrate only a short distance and interact strongly with surface atoms (and cause less damage).

practice.stem: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from the energy level at −1.51 eV to the level at −3.40 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy of the photon emitted, in eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the emitted light and state its colour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a hot, low-pressure gas produces an emission line spectrum.
parts.answer: Electrons in the atoms are excited to higher energy levels; they fall to lower levels, emitting photons; each photon's energy equals the difference between two discrete levels, hf = E₁ − E₂, so only certain frequencies appear.
parts.working: B1 excitation; B1 de-excitation emits photon; B1 discrete levels give discrete frequencies/hf = ΔE

parts.label: b
parts.text: White light passes through a cool gas. Explain why the spectrum of the transmitted light contains dark lines.
parts.answer: Atoms absorb photons whose energies exactly equal differences between their energy levels; these are re-emitted in all directions, so those wavelengths are missing (much weaker) in the forward beam.
parts.working: B1 absorb photons of energy = ΔE only; B1 re-emitted in all directions

practice.stem: Four energy levels of the hydrogen atom are −13.6 eV (ground state), −3.40 eV, −1.51 eV and −0.85 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of different photon energies that can be emitted as atoms in the −0.85 eV level return to the ground state by any route.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the shortest wavelength emitted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the energy levels are given negative values.
parts.answer: Zero energy is defined for an electron that is free of the atom (at infinity); a bound electron has less energy than this.

practice.stem: An electron with kinetic energy 12.2 eV collides with a hydrogen atom in its ground state. Energy levels of hydrogen: −13.6 eV, −3.40 eV, −1.51 eV, −0.85 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which energy levels the hydrogen atom can be excited to by the collision. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: To −3.40 eV (needs 10.2 eV) or −1.51 eV (needs 12.09 eV), not −0.85 eV (needs 12.75 eV, more than 12.2 eV). Unlike photons, an electron can give up only part of its energy.
parts.working: B1 levels −3.40 and −1.51 eV; B1 12.75 eV > 12.2 eV / electron can transfer part of its energy

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the electron after it excites an atom to the highest possible level.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the wavelengths of all the photons that could then be emitted.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A car accelerates uniformly from 4.0 m s⁻¹ to 22 m s⁻¹ in a time of 6.0 s. What is the distance travelled in this time?
A 54 m
B 78 m
C 108 m
D 132 m
parts.working: s = ½(u + v)t = ½(4.0 + 22) × 6.0 = 78 m. 132 m wrongly uses the final speed for the whole time; 54 m uses only ½Δv × t and ignores the initial speed.

practice.stem: A motorcycle starts from rest at a traffic signal in Lahore and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻² along a straight road for 8.0 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by acceleration.
parts.working: B1: change of velocity ÷ time taken (rate of change of velocity). 'Speed' instead of velocity scores 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the motorcycle at the end of the 8.0 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the distance travelled by the motorcycle in the 8.0 s.

practice.stem: A local train travels in a straight line between two stations. Its velocity–time graph is made of straight lines joining these points (time in s, velocity in m s⁻¹): (0, 0), (40, 16), (160, 16), (200, 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the train during the first 40 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the total distance travelled between the two stations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average speed of the train for the whole journey.

practice.stem: A lift in an office tower starts from rest and accelerates upwards uniformly at 1.2 m s⁻² for 2.5 s. It then moves at constant speed for 9.0 s and finally decelerates uniformly to rest in 2.0 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the lift.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total height risen by the lift.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A stone is dropped from rest from a high bridge and falls freely for 3.0 s. Air resistance is negligible and g = 9.81 m s⁻². How far does it fall?
A 14.7 m
B 29.4 m
C 44.1 m
D 88.3 m
parts.working: s = ½gt² = ½ × 9.81 × 9.0 = 44.1 m. 29.4 m is gt (the final speed in m s⁻¹), not a distance; 88.3 m omits the ½.

practice.stem: A cyclist rides 4.2 km due north along a straight road in 10 min, then turns and rides 3.0 km due south in 5 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between speed and velocity.
parts.answer: Speed is a scalar (distance per unit time); velocity is a vector (displacement per unit time, with direction).
parts.working: B1: velocity has direction / is a vector (rate of change of displacement); speed is scalar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average speed of the cyclist for the whole 15 min.
parts.working: Total distance 7200 m, total time 900 s (M1); 7200/900 = 8.0 m s⁻¹ (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average velocity of the cyclist for the whole 15 min.
parts.working: Displacement = 4.2 − 3.0 = 1.2 km north (M1); 1200/900 = 1.33 m s⁻¹ north (A1; direction needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An object moving in a straight line with uniform acceleration has a velocity of 5.0 m s⁻¹. After travelling a further 24 m its velocity is 11 m s⁻¹. What is its acceleration?
A 0.25 m s⁻²
B 2.0 m s⁻²
C 2.5 m s⁻²
D 4.0 m s⁻²
parts.working: v² = u² + 2as → a = (121 − 25)/(2 × 24) = 2.0 m s⁻². 4.0 m s⁻² forgets the factor 2; 0.25 m s⁻² divides the change in speed by the distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards and is caught again at the same height. Air resistance is negligible. Upwards is taken as positive. Which statement describes the acceleration–time graph of the ball while it is in the air?
A a horizontal line at a negative value
B a sloping straight line from a positive value to a negative value
C a horizontal line at zero, because the ball returns to its starting point
D a horizontal line at a positive value until the top, then at a negative value
parts.answer: A a horizontal line at a negative value
parts.working: The only force is weight, so acceleration is g downwards (−9.81 m s⁻²) throughout, including at the top. The sloping line describes the velocity–time graph, not acceleration.

practice.stem: A driver on the M-2 motorway is travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ when he sees an obstruction. His reaction time is 0.65 s. The brakes then give a uniform deceleration of 6.5 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the thinking distance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the braking distance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the total stopping distance.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the stopping distance more than doubles when the initial speed is doubled.
parts.answer: Thinking distance doubles (∝ u) but braking distance quadruples (∝ u²).
parts.working: B1: thinking distance ∝ u so doubles; B1: braking distance ∝ u² so becomes four times as large, so total more than doubles.

practice.stem:
A trolley is released from rest on a slope. Its displacement s along the slope is recorded at time t:
t / s: 0, 0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00
s / m: 0, 0.10, 0.40, 0.90, 1.60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the data are consistent with uniform acceleration from rest.
parts.answer: s/t² is constant (0.40 m s⁻²) for every reading, so s ∝ t².
parts.working: M1: calculate s/t² for at least three readings (0.40, 0.40, 0.40, 0.40); A1: constant, so s = ½at² with constant a (starting from rest, s = 0 at t = 0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the acceleration of the trolley.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the velocity of the trolley at t = 2.0 s.

practice.stem: A tennis ball is dropped from rest from a height of 1.8 m onto a hard floor. It leaves the floor with 70% of the speed it had just before impact. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the ball just before it hits the floor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the height reached by the ball after the bounce.
parts.working: Rebound speed 0.70 × 5.94 = 4.16 m s⁻¹ (M1); h = v²/2g = 0.882 m (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Taking downwards as positive, describe the velocity–time graph of the ball from release until it reaches the top of its first bounce.
parts.answer: Straight line from 0 rising to +5.94 m s⁻¹; near-vertical drop to −4.16 m s⁻¹ at the bounce; straight line from −4.16 m s⁻¹ back to 0, parallel to the first line.
parts.working: B1: straight line through origin with positive gradient (9.81 m s⁻²) to +5.94; B1: sudden change to a negative velocity of smaller magnitude at impact; B1: second line has the same gradient as the first and ends at v = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A car decelerates uniformly from 30 m s⁻¹ to rest over a distance of 75 m. How long does it take to stop?
A 2.5 s
B 5.0 s
C 6.0 s
D 10 s
parts.working: s = ½(u + v)t → t = 2s/(u + v) = 150/30 = 5.0 s. 2.5 s comes from s/u, which assumes constant speed of 30 m s⁻¹ throughout.

practice.stem:
A student releases a trolley from rest at the top of a ramp and measures the time t for it to travel a distance d down the ramp to a light gate. The results are:
d = 0.200 m, t = 0.86 s
d = 0.400 m, t = 1.20 s
d = 0.600 m, t = 1.48 s
d = 0.800 m, t = 1.72 s
d = 1.000 m, t = 1.90 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate t² for each reading, giving each value to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: B1 all values correct; B1 all given to 3 s.f. as asked (the raw times are recorded to 0.01 s).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a graph of d against t² should be a straight line through the origin, and state what the gradient represents.
parts.answer: d = ½at² with u = 0, so d ∝ t²; gradient = a/2.
parts.working: B1: d = ½at² (from rest); B1: gradient = ½a.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The best-fit line through the origin has gradient 0.274 m s⁻². Calculate the acceleration of the trolley.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one significant source of error in this experiment and one improvement to reduce it.
parts.answer: e.g. trolley not released exactly from rest / starting position unclear; use a release gate or electromagnet, or use light gates and data logger to measure t.
parts.working: B1 valid source (human reaction time starting the stopwatch, trolley pushed at release, friction varies along ramp); B1 matching improvement (electronic timing with light gates, release mechanism, repeat and average).

practice.stem: A car starts from rest at t = 0. Its acceleration a varies with time as follows: a = 3.0 m s⁻² from t = 0 to t = 4.0 s; a = 0 from t = 4.0 s to t = 10.0 s; a = −2.0 m s⁻² from t = 10.0 s to t = 13.0 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the velocity of the car at t = 4.0 s and at t = 13.0 s.
parts.working: Velocity change = area under a–t graph (M1): 3.0 × 4.0 = 12 m s⁻¹; 12 − 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 m s⁻¹ (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total distance travelled by the car in the 13.0 s.

practice.stem: A car decelerating uniformly in a straight line passes point P at 28 m s⁻¹ and point Q, 120 m further on, at 20 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the deceleration of the car.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken to travel from P to Q.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The car continues to decelerate at the same rate after Q. Calculate how much further it travels before it stops.

practice.stem: A student drops a small stone from rest at the top of a deep well in a village in Sindh. She hears the splash 2.40 s after release. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assume the sound reaches the student instantly. Calculate the depth of the water surface below the top of the well.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. Taking this into account, calculate the depth of the water surface.
parts.working: Let fall time = t. t + ½gt²/340 = 2.40 (M1). Solve the quadratic 0.014426t² + t − 2.40 = 0 (M1): t = 2.32 s, so depth = ½ × 9.81 × t² = 26.5 m (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one other assumption made in your calculations and say whether it makes your answer to (b) too large or too small.
parts.answer: Air resistance on the stone is negligible; ignoring it makes the calculated depth too large.
parts.working: B1: air resistance ignored → stone actually falls more slowly, so true depth is less than calculated (calculated value too large). Accept also reaction time of student with a valid direction.

practice.stem: A bus moves along a straight road at a constant speed of 18 m s⁻¹. As it passes a stationary police car, the police car sets off from rest in the same direction with a constant acceleration of 2.4 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the police car to draw level with the bus.
parts.working: Same displacement: 18t = ½ × 2.4 × t² (M1); t ≠ 0 so t = 2×18/2.4 (M1) = 15 s (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance travelled by each vehicle in this time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the police car when it draws level, and comment on how it compares with the speed of the bus.
parts.answer: 36 m s⁻¹, twice the speed of the bus
parts.working: v = at = 2.4 × 15 = 36 m s⁻¹ (A1); exactly twice 18 m s⁻¹ because the average speed of the car (½v) must equal 18 m s⁻¹ (B1).

practice.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 12 m s⁻¹ from a balcony 15 m above the ground. It misses the balcony on the way down and lands on the ground. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum height of the ball above the ground.
parts.working: Rise above balcony = u²/2g = 144/19.62 = 7.34 m (M1); height = 15 + 7.34 = 22.3 m (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time from release until the ball hits the ground.
parts.working: Up positive: −15 = 12t − 4.905t² (M1); 4.905t² − 12t − 15 = 0 (M1); positive root t = 3.36 s (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the ball just before it hits the ground.

practice.stem: A metro train runs between two stations 3.60 km apart on a straight track. It starts and ends at rest. Its maximum acceleration is 0.80 m s⁻², its maximum deceleration is 1.2 m s⁻² and its top speed is 25 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance travelled while the train accelerates to its top speed and the distance travelled while it decelerates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the minimum time for the journey.
parts.working: Acceleration time 31.3 s, deceleration time 20.8 s (M1); cruising distance 3600 − 651 = 2949 m → 118.0 s (M1); total 170 s (A1).

practice.stem: A model rocket is launched vertically from rest at a school science fair. It accelerates uniformly upwards at 15 m s⁻² for 6.0 s, when its fuel runs out. It then moves freely under gravity. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed and the height of the rocket when the fuel runs out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum height reached by the rocket.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total time from launch until the rocket hits the ground.

practice.stem: A boy on a cliff at Gwadar throws a stone horizontally at 8.0 m s⁻¹ from a point 20 m above the sea. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the stone to reach the sea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff to where the stone lands.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the horizontal component of the stone's velocity stays constant.
parts.answer: There is no horizontal force (air resistance negligible), so no horizontal acceleration.
parts.working: B1: no horizontal force / gravity acts vertically only.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A ball is projected at an angle above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. Which quantity remains constant during its flight?
A its kinetic energy
B its speed
C the horizontal component of its velocity
D the vertical component of its velocity
parts.answer: C the horizontal component of its velocity
parts.working: Gravity acts only vertically, so the horizontal velocity component does not change. The vertical component changes at 9.81 m s⁻² each second, so speed and kinetic energy also change.

practice.stem: A footballer kicks a ball from the ground at 15 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the magnitude and direction of the acceleration of the ball at its highest point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the ball to reach its highest point.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the speed of the ball at its highest point.
parts.working: Vertical component zero, so speed = horizontal component = 13.0 m s⁻¹ (B1).

practice.stem: During a cricket match in Rawalpindi a batter hits the ball from ground level at 25 m s⁻¹ at 35° above the horizontal. Treat the ball as starting at ground level and ignore air resistance; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum height reached by the ball.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal distance travelled before the ball returns to ground level.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ball X is dropped from rest from the edge of a high table. At the same instant ball Y, of twice the mass, is projected horizontally at 3 m s⁻¹ from the same height. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement is correct?
A X reaches the floor first because it travels a shorter distance.
B Y reaches the floor first because it has a greater mass.
C Both reach the floor at the same time, with the same speed.
D Both reach the floor at the same time, but Y has the greater speed.
parts.answer: D Both reach the floor at the same time, but Y has the greater speed.
parts.working: Both have zero initial vertical velocity and acceleration g, so equal fall times and equal vertical speeds on landing. Y also has 3 m s⁻¹ horizontally, so its speed is greater. C forgets the horizontal component.

practice.stem: A decorative fountain in a park in Islamabad has a nozzle that sends water out at 9.0 m s⁻¹ at 60° above the horizontal. Treat the water as a projectile with no air resistance; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum height of the water above the nozzle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal distance from the nozzle to where the water returns to the level of the nozzle.
parts.working: Time = 2uᵧ/g = 1.59 s (M1); uₓ = 9.0 cos 60° = 4.50 m s⁻¹ (M1); distance 7.15 m (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The nozzle angle is changed to 30° with the same speed. State, with a reason, how the horizontal distance in (b) changes.
parts.answer: It stays the same, because sin(2 × 30°) = sin(2 × 60°).
parts.working: B1: range ∝ sin 2θ and sin 60° = sin 120°, so same range (but lower maximum height).

practice.stem: A marble rolls off the edge of a horizontal laboratory bench of height 0.90 m and lands on the floor 1.10 m horizontally from the edge of the bench. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the marble to fall to the floor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the marble as it leaves the table.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the marble just before it hits the floor.

practice.stem: An athlete releases a javelin at a height of 1.8 m above level ground with a speed of 28 m s⁻¹ at 40° above the horizontal. Treat the javelin as a particle; ignore air resistance unless told otherwise; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time for which the javelin is in the air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal distance travelled.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In reality air resistance acts on the javelin. State and explain two ways in which the actual path differs from the path you have calculated.
parts.answer: Lower maximum height and shorter range; the path is not symmetrical — it falls more steeply after the highest point.
parts.working: B1 each for any two: range less (horizontal velocity decreases); maximum height lower (extra downward force while rising); highest point reached sooner / path asymmetric, descending more steeply.

practice.stem: A basketball player releases a ball 2.00 m above the floor at 50° above the horizontal. The centre of the hoop is 3.05 m above the floor and 6.00 m horizontally from the release point. Ignore air resistance and the size of the ball; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the equation of the path is y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u² cos² θ), where y is the height above the release point after a horizontal distance x.
parts.answer: x = (u cos θ)t, y = (u sin θ)t − ½gt²; eliminate t.
parts.working: M1: t = x/(u cos θ); A1: substitute into y = u sin θ t − ½gt² to give the result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the launch speed needed for the ball to pass through the centre of the hoop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time the ball takes to reach the hoop.

practice.stem: During flood relief work, a light aircraft flying horizontally at 60 m s⁻¹ at a height of 245 m releases a food package so that it lands on a marked target. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal distance before the target at which the package must be released.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the package just before it lands and the angle its velocity makes with the horizontal.
parts.answer: 91.7 m s⁻¹ at 49.1° below the horizontal

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the position of the package relative to the aircraft as it falls, assuming the aircraft keeps the same velocity and air resistance is negligible.
parts.answer: It stays vertically below the aircraft.
parts.working: B1: same horizontal velocity as the aircraft, so always directly below it.

practice.stem: A hydrogen spectral line has a wavelength of 656.3 nm when measured in a laboratory. In the spectrum of light from a distant galaxy, the same line is observed at 669.4 nm. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by redshift.
parts.answer: The increase in the observed wavelength (decrease in frequency) of electromagnetic radiation because the source is moving away from the observer.
parts.working: B1 increase in wavelength / decrease in frequency due to the source receding

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which the galaxy is moving away from the Earth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Hubble constant is 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Calculate the distance to the galaxy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Hubble's law.
parts.answer: The recession speed of a galaxy is (approximately) proportional to its distance from the Earth: v ≈ H₀d.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the redshift of light from distant galaxies leads to the idea that the Universe is expanding.
parts.answer: Light from (almost) all distant galaxies is redshifted, so they are all moving away from us; the further away a galaxy is, the greater its redshift (speed), as expected if space itself is expanding.
parts.working: B1 (almost) all distant galaxies show redshift so are receding; B1 recession speed increases with distance (Hubble's law), so the Universe is expanding

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how an expanding Universe supports the Big Bang theory.
parts.answer: If galaxies are moving apart now, they were closer together in the past; tracing back, the whole Universe was once concentrated in an extremely small, hot, dense region from which it expanded.
parts.working: B1 galaxies were closer together in the past; B1 Universe began from a single point / very small, hot, dense state (Big Bang)

practice.stem: Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Andromeda galaxy is moving towards the Milky Way at 300 km s⁻¹. Calculate the observed wavelength of the 656.3 nm hydrogen line in its spectrum.
parts.working: Δλ = λv/c = 656.3 × 3.00 × 10⁵/3.00 × 10⁸ = 0.656 nm (C1); approaching so λ decreases: 655.6 nm (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name given to this shift.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why Andromeda's motion does not contradict the idea that the Universe is expanding.
parts.answer: Andromeda is very close, so the gravitational attraction between the galaxies is greater than the effect of expansion; Hubble's law applies to distant galaxies.

practice.stem: A galaxy is moving away from the Earth at 2.1 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. A spectral line from hydrogen has a laboratory wavelength of 486.1 nm. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fractional change in wavelength Δλ/λ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the observed wavelength of the line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the observed frequency compares with the laboratory frequency.

practice.stem: A recent value of the Hubble constant H₀ is 68 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that 68 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ is about 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming that galaxies have always moved apart at their present speeds, the age of the Universe is approximately 1/H₀. Explain why.
parts.answer: A galaxy at distance d moving at v = H₀d has taken t = d/v = 1/H₀ to travel from the starting point, the same for every galaxy.
parts.working: B1 time = distance/speed; B1 d/v = d/(H₀d) = 1/H₀, independent of d

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the age of the Universe in years. (1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s)

practice.stem: Radio telescopes detect the 21 cm emission from hydrogen gas, which has a frequency of 1420 MHz in the laboratory. From one galaxy this radiation is received at a frequency of 1385 MHz. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the observed frequency is consistent with a redshift, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Yes: the observed frequency is lower, so the wavelength is longer (redshift).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of recession of the galaxy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹, calculate the distance to the galaxy in Mpc. (1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m)

practice.stem: A galaxy is 150 Mpc from the Earth. Take the Hubble constant as 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. A calcium absorption line has a wavelength of 393.4 nm in the laboratory. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the recession speed of the galaxy in km s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength at which this calcium line is observed in the galaxy's spectrum.

practice.stem: Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A galaxy has Δλ/λ = 0.050. Calculate its recession speed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The relation Δλ/λ ≈ v/c is an approximation. State the condition for it to be valid.
parts.answer: The speed of the source must be much less than the speed of light (v ≪ c).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Light from a very distant quasar has Δλ/λ = 2.0. Explain why the equation cannot be used to find the quasar's speed.
parts.answer: It would give v = 2c, which is impossible; at such large redshifts v is not ≪ c, so the approximation fails.
parts.working: B1 gives v greater than c; B1 approximation only valid for v ≪ c

practice.stem: An oxygen emission line with a laboratory wavelength of 500.7 nm is observed at 515.7 nm in the spectrum of a galaxy. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the recession speed and the distance of the galaxy, using H₀ = 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how long, in years, the light has taken to reach the Earth. Ignore the expansion of the Universe during the light's journey. (1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why astronomers say that observing very distant galaxies is like looking back in time.
parts.answer: The light left the galaxy long ago, so we see the galaxy as it was when the light was emitted.

practice.stem:
An astronomer measures the distance d and recession speed v of five galaxies.

d/Mpc: 20, 45, 80, 120, 160
v/km s⁻¹: 1350, 3200, 5500, 8600, 11 000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph of v against d can be used to test Hubble's law, and state what the gradient represents.
parts.answer: Hubble's law v = H₀d predicts a straight line through the origin; gradient = H₀.
parts.working: B1 straight line through origin expected; B1 gradient = H₀

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the gradient of the best-fit line using the first and last data points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert your value of H₀ into s⁻¹ and hence estimate the age of the Universe in years. (1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m, 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s)

parts.label: d
parts.text: The distances have uncertainties of about ±10 %. Suggest two reasons why distances to galaxies are hard to measure accurately.
parts.answer: Any two of: the luminosity of standard candles must be calibrated and is known only approximately; dust absorbs light, reducing the measured radiant flux; individual stars (e.g. Cepheids) in distant galaxies are faint and hard to resolve; the radiant flux of faint objects is hard to measure precisely.
parts.working: B1 each for any two sensible reasons relating to distance measurement (not to the recession speed)

practice.stem: The fractional changes in wavelength Δλ/λ of a spectral line from two galaxies A and B are 0.012 and 0.036. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the ratio of the distances of the galaxies can be found without knowing the Hubble constant, and state its value.
parts.working: M1 Δλ/λ = v/c and v = H₀d so d ∝ Δλ/λ; A1 3.0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Galaxy A is found from Cepheid variable stars to be 52 Mpc away. Determine the Hubble constant in km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the distance to galaxy B, and explain why astronomers rely on redshift, rather than Cepheids, for galaxies much further away than B.
parts.answer: 156 Mpc. Cepheids in very distant galaxies are too faint to be resolved/measured, but spectral lines (and hence redshift) can still be measured.
parts.working: B1 156 Mpc; B1 individual Cepheids too faint at large distances

practice.stem: A Type Ia supernova is observed in a distant galaxy. At its peak, its luminosity is known to be 2.0 × 10³⁶ W and the radiant flux intensity measured at the Earth is 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ W m⁻². Spectral lines from the galaxy show Δλ/λ = 0.0140. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance to the galaxy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the recession speed of the galaxy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine a value for the Hubble constant in s⁻¹.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why values of H₀ from many galaxies at different distances are needed for a reliable result.
parts.answer: Individual galaxies have their own random (peculiar) velocities and distance errors; averaging/a graph of many galaxies reduces their effect.

practice.stem: Take the Wien's displacement law constant λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Wien's displacement law.
parts.answer: The wavelength at which a black body emits maximum power is inversely proportional to its thermodynamic temperature: λ_max ∝ 1/T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The spectrum of the Sun has its peak intensity at a wavelength of about 500 nm. Estimate the surface temperature of the Sun.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the assumption made about the Sun in (b).
parts.answer: It behaves as a black body.

practice.stem: Take the Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the Stefan–Boltzmann law for a star of radius r and surface temperature T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A star has a radius of 2.1 × 10⁹ m and a surface temperature of 7500 K. Calculate its luminosity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the meaning of luminosity.
parts.answer: The total power of electromagnetic radiation emitted by the star.

practice.stem: Take the Wien's displacement law constant λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the surface temperature of a star can be found from its spectrum.
parts.answer: Measure the intensity of the star's radiation at different wavelengths and find the wavelength λ_max at which it is greatest; then T = (2.9 × 10⁻³ m K)/λ_max (Wien's law).
parts.working: B1 find wavelength of maximum intensity from the spectrum; B1 use Wien's law λ_max T = constant

parts.label: b
parts.text: The spectrum of a star peaks at 420 nm. Calculate its surface temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether this star is hotter or cooler than the Sun (peak at about 500 nm), giving a reason.
parts.answer: Hotter, because its peak wavelength is shorter (λ_max ∝ 1/T).

practice.stem: A red supergiant star has a luminosity of 4.0 × 10³¹ W. The peak of its emission spectrum is at a wavelength of 850 nm. Take the Wien's displacement law constant λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K. Take the Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface temperature of the star.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the radius of the star.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The radius of the Earth's orbit is 1.5 × 10¹¹ m. Comment on the size of this star.
parts.answer: Its radius is about 4.3 times the Earth–Sun distance: if placed at the Sun it would extend beyond the Earth's orbit.

practice.stem: A white dwarf star has a surface temperature of 25 000 K and a luminosity of 2.1 × 10²⁵ W. Take the Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. Take the Wien's displacement law constant λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the radius of the white dwarf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength at which its emission peaks and state the region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Earth has a radius of 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Explain why white dwarfs are very hot but have low luminosity.
parts.answer: The white dwarf is about the size of the Earth: its surface area is tiny, so although T⁴ is large, L = 4πσr²T⁴ is small.
parts.working: B1 radius comparable to Earth's; B1 small surface area outweighs high T in L = 4πσr²T⁴

practice.stem: The Sun has a radius of 6.96 × 10⁸ m and a surface temperature of 5800 K. Take the Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the luminosity of the Sun is about 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the radiant flux intensity of the Sun's radiation at the Earth, 1.50 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the intensity measured by a solar panel on a roof in Multan at midday is less than your answer to (b).
parts.answer: Some radiation is absorbed/scattered by the atmosphere (and the panel may not face the Sun directly).

practice.stem:
The table shows the wavelength λ_max at which five model stars emit their maximum power, and their surface temperatures T.

λ_max/nm: 966, 725, 580, 414, 290
T/K: 3000, 4000, 5000, 7000, 10000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest what graph should be plotted to test whether λ_max is inversely proportional to T, and describe the expected result.
parts.answer: Plot λ_max against 1/T: a straight line through the origin is expected.
parts.working: B1 λ_max against 1/T (or λ_max T for each star); B1 straight line through origin (or constant product)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate λ_max T for each star and state whether the data support the relationship.
parts.answer: λ_max T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K for every star (2.898 to 2.900 × 10⁻³), so the data support λ_max ∝ 1/T.
parts.working: B1 all products correct ≈ 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K; B1 constant, so supported

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the surface temperature of a star whose spectrum peaks at 1.16 µm.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the surface temperatures of real stars found in this way have significant uncertainties.
parts.answer: Stars are not perfect black bodies / absorption in the star's atmosphere or by dust changes the spectrum / the peak is broad and hard to locate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Star P and star Q have the same luminosity. The surface temperature of P is twice that of Q. Determine the ratio (radius of P)/(radius of Q).
parts.working: M1 L ∝ r²T⁴ with L the same, so r ∝ 1/T²; A1 r_P/r_Q = 1/2² = 0.25

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the ratio (λ_max for P)/(λ_max for Q).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Star R has the same radius as Q but λ_max for R is 1.5 times λ_max for Q. Determine the ratio (luminosity of R)/(luminosity of Q).

practice.stem: A nearby bright star is 8.6 light-years from the Earth. The radiant flux intensity of its radiation at the Earth is 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻² and the peak of its spectrum is at 290 nm. 1 light-year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. Take the Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. Take the Wien's displacement law constant λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the luminosity of the star.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the surface temperature of the star.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the radius of the star.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this method gives only an estimate of the radius.
parts.answer: The star is not a perfect black body / the peak wavelength and the flux (affected by absorption) are hard to measure precisely.

practice.stem: Near the end of its life a star like the Sun becomes a red giant. Suppose its radius increases by a factor of 100 and its surface temperature halves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the factor by which the luminosity of the star changes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the factor by which the peak wavelength of its spectrum changes, and describe the change in the star's colour.
parts.answer: λ_max doubles; the star appears redder.
parts.working: B1 λ_max ∝ 1/T, so ×2; B1 shifts towards red/infrared (redder)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a star can become more luminous even though its surface becomes cooler.
parts.answer: The large increase in surface area (r² × 10 000) outweighs the decrease in T⁴ (÷16).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the luminosity of a star.
parts.answer: The total power of electromagnetic radiation emitted by the star.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by the radiant flux intensity of a star at the Earth.
parts.answer: The radiant power passing normally through unit area at the Earth (W m⁻²).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by a standard candle.
parts.answer: An astronomical object of known luminosity.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how a standard candle can be used to find the distance to a galaxy containing it.
parts.answer: Measure its radiant flux intensity F at the Earth; since L is known, use F = L/(4πd²) to calculate d = √(L/(4πF)).
parts.working: B1 measure F; B1 use inverse-square law with known L to find d

practice.stem: The luminosity of the Sun is 3.83 × 10²⁶ W. Mars is 2.28 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the radiant flux intensity of the Sun's radiation at Mars.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the radiant flux intensity decreases with the square of the distance from the Sun.
parts.answer: The same power spreads out over the surface of a sphere of area 4πd², which increases as d²; so power per unit area ∝ 1/d².
parts.working: B1 power spread over sphere of area 4πd²; B1 hence F ∝ 1/d² (no absorption)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two types of standard candle used by astronomers.
parts.answer: Cepheid variable stars; Type Ia supernovae

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each type, state how its luminosity is known.
parts.answer: Cepheids: luminosity is found from the period of their brightness variation (period–luminosity relation). Type Ia supernovae: all reach (almost) the same peak luminosity.
parts.working: B1 Cepheid period–luminosity; B1 Type Ia same peak luminosity

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which type is used to measure the greater distances, and why.
parts.answer: Type Ia supernovae, because they are much more luminous and visible from much further away.

practice.stem: A Cepheid variable star in a nearby galaxy has a period which shows that its luminosity is 1.2 × 10³⁰ W. Its radiant flux intensity at the Earth is 3.5 × 10⁻¹³ W m⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the period of a Cepheid variable star is measured.
parts.answer: The period is related to its luminosity (period–luminosity relation), so measuring the period gives L.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance to the Cepheid, in m and in light-years. (1 light-year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Interstellar dust between the Cepheid and the Earth absorbs some of its light. State and explain the effect on the calculated distance.
parts.answer: The distance is overestimated: the measured flux is smaller than it would be, and d ∝ 1/√F.
parts.working: B1 calculated distance too large; B1 F reduced and d ∝ F^(−1/2)

practice.stem: Two stars A and B are of the same type and have the same luminosity. The radiant flux intensity of star A at the Earth is 25 times that of star B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the ratio (distance of star B)/(distance of star A).
parts.working: M1 same L, so F ∝ 1/d², d ∝ 1/√F; A1 √25 = 5.0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Star A is 40 pc from the Earth. State the distance of star B in pc and in metres. (1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the assumption that allows these two stars to be compared in this way.
parts.answer: They have the same luminosity (they are standard candles of the same type), and no light is absorbed on the way.

practice.stem: The radiant flux intensity of the Sun's radiation just above the Earth's atmosphere is 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻². The Earth is 1.50 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the luminosity of the Sun.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Neptune is 4.50 × 10¹² m from the Sun. Calculate the radiant flux intensity of sunlight at Neptune.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a space probe sent to Neptune does not use solar panels as its main power source.
parts.answer: The intensity there is about 1/900 of that at the Earth, so solar panels would produce far too little power.

practice.stem: A Type Ia supernova reaches a peak luminosity of 2.0 × 10³⁶ W. The peak radiant flux intensity measured at the Earth is 6.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ W m⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance to the supernova in Mpc. (1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Later observations show that 20 % of the light was absorbed by dust in the host galaxy. Determine the true distance in Mpc, and the percentage by which your answer to (a) was in error.
parts.answer: true distance = 149 Mpc; (a) was 12 % too large
parts.working: C1 true F = 6.0 × 10⁻¹⁵/0.80 = 7.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ W m⁻²; A1 d = 149 Mpc; A1 ratio = 1/√0.80 = 1.12, so 12 % too large

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Type Ia supernovae are used rather than Cepheids for galaxies at this distance.
parts.answer: Type Ia supernovae are far more luminous, so they can still be detected (and measured) at distances where Cepheids are too faint.

practice.stem: A Cepheid in the Milky Way, at a known distance of 2.5 kpc, has the same period as a Cepheid in a distant galaxy. Their radiant flux intensities at the Earth are 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹ W m⁻² and 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁷ W m⁻² respectively.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the two Cepheids can be assumed to have the same luminosity.
parts.answer: Cepheids with the same period have the same luminosity (period–luminosity relation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the distance to the galaxy, in kpc and in Mpc.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The distance to the nearby Cepheid is uncertain by ±4 %. State the percentage uncertainty in the distance to the galaxy, ignoring other uncertainties, and explain why accurate calibration of nearby standard candles is so important.
parts.answer: ±4 %; every distance found using that type of standard candle (and hence H₀) depends on the calibration, so its error carries through to all of them.
parts.working: B1 ±4 % (d_far ∝ d_near); B1 calibration error propagates to all distances measured this way

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student uses a micrometer screw gauge to measure the diameter of a wire. She does not notice that the gauge reads +0.03 mm when its jaws are closed. Which statement about her readings is correct?
A They have a random error, so they are precise but not accurate.
B They have a systematic error, so they may be precise but are not accurate.
C They have a random error that can be removed by averaging many readings.
D They have a systematic error that can be removed by averaging many readings.
parts.answer: B They have a systematic error, so they may be precise but are not accurate.
parts.working: A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount: a systematic error. Readings can still be close together (precise) but are all wrong by 0.03 mm (not accurate). Averaging (C, D) reduces random error only, not a systematic one.

practice.stem: A student in Multan measures a cylindrical pencil. Its length L is 14.6 ± 0.1 cm (metre rule) and its diameter d is 7.12 ± 0.01 mm (micrometer).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the length.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the diameter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The volume of the pencil is V = πd²L/4. Calculate V in cm³ and its absolute uncertainty.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a systematic error and a random error.
parts.answer: Systematic: readings all differ from the true value by the same amount or in the same direction. Random: readings scatter unpredictably either side of the true value.
parts.working: B1: systematic error – same size/same sign for every reading (e.g. zero error); B1: random error – scatter of readings about the mean, different each time

parts.label: b
parts.text:
For each of the following, state whether it causes a systematic or a random error and suggest how it can be reduced.
(i) An electronic balance reads 0.4 g with nothing on its pan.
(ii) A student's reaction time varies when starting and stopping a stopwatch to time a falling ball.
parts.answer: (i) systematic – take the zero reading and subtract it from every reading (or tare the balance). (ii) random – repeat and average, or use light gates connected to a timer.
parts.working: B1 systematic; B1 correct for zero error/tare; B1 random; B1 repeat and average or use light gates/video with timer

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Five readings of the diameter of a wire are 2.43 mm, 2.45 mm, 2.41 mm, 2.46 mm and 2.44 mm. Which value and uncertainty best represent these readings?
A 2.44 ± 0.01 mm
B 2.44 ± 0.03 mm
C 2.44 ± 0.05 mm
D 2.438 ± 0.005 mm
parts.working: Mean = 12.19/5 = 2.438 ≈ 2.44 mm; uncertainty = half the range = (2.46 − 2.41)/2 = 0.025 ≈ 0.03 mm. C uses the full range; D quotes too many s.f.

practice.stem: In a laboratory in Lahore, the length L of a simple pendulum is 0.865 ± 0.002 m. The time for 20 oscillations is 37.4 ± 0.2 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period T of the pendulum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The acceleration of free fall is given by g = 4π²L/T². Calculate g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the absolute uncertainty in g and write g with its uncertainty to an appropriate number of significant figures.

practice.stem: The potential difference across a lamp is 6.24 ± 0.05 V and the current in it is 0.320 ± 0.004 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance R of the lamp filament.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the absolute uncertainty in R.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which of the two meter readings contributes more to the uncertainty in R. Explain your answer.
parts.working: Its percentage uncertainty (1.25 %) is larger than that of the voltage (0.80 %) (B1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A quantity X is calculated from X = a²b/√c. The percentage uncertainties are 2 % in a, 3 % in b and 4 % in c. What is the percentage uncertainty in X?
A 5 %
B 7 %
C 9 %
D 11 %
parts.working: %X = 2 × 2 + 3 + ½ × 4 = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9 %. 11 % comes from using 4 % for c without halving it.

practice.stem:
The accepted value of g in a city is 9.81 m s⁻². Two students measure g.
Student A: 9.62, 9.63, 9.61, 9.62 m s⁻²
Student B: 9.70, 9.95, 9.85, 9.74 m s⁻²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean value of g for each student.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State, with reasons, which set of results is more precise and which is more accurate.
parts.answer: A is more precise (small spread); B is more accurate (mean equals the accepted value).
parts.working: B1 A precise – readings close together; B1 B accurate – mean close to 9.81 m s⁻²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what type of error is present in student A's results.
parts.answer: A systematic error (e.g. length measured to the wrong point of the bob).

practice.stem: A steel ball bearing from a bicycle workshop has mass m = 28.4 ± 0.1 g. Its diameter d is measured with vernier calipers as 1.90 ± 0.02 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the density of the ball is about 7.9 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the absolute uncertainty in the density.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest, with a reason, which measurement should be made more precisely to reduce the uncertainty in the density most effectively.
parts.answer: The diameter, e.g. using a micrometer or digital calipers.
parts.working: B1 diameter; B1 its percentage uncertainty is multiplied by 3 / it dominates the total

practice.stem: A spring has length 24.3 ± 0.1 cm when unloaded. When a weight of 4.00 ± 0.02 N hangs from it, its length is 31.8 ± 0.1 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the extension of the spring and its absolute uncertainty.
parts.working: x = 31.8 − 24.3 = 7.5 cm (B1); uncertainties add when subtracting: 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 cm (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the spring constant k and its absolute uncertainty.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the percentage uncertainty in the extension is much larger than that in either length reading.
parts.answer: The extension is a small difference of two similar lengths, but the absolute uncertainties add.

practice.stem: A trolley of mass 0.250 ± 0.002 kg travels at constant speed. It covers 1.500 ± 0.005 m in a time measured with a stopwatch as 0.62 ± 0.02 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed v of the trolley.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the trolley.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the absolute uncertainty in the kinetic energy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one change to the experiment that would reduce the uncertainty in E most effectively.
parts.answer: Measure the time with light gates and an electronic timer (or use a longer distance).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is an SI base unit?
A newton
B coulomb
C kelvin
D volt
parts.working: The kelvin is one of the base units (with kg, m, s, A, mol). The coulomb is a derived unit (A s), a common distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a base quantity and a derived quantity.
parts.answer: A base quantity is one of the chosen fundamental quantities (e.g. mass, length, time); a derived quantity is defined in terms of base quantities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the unit of pressure, the pascal, is kg m⁻¹ s⁻² in SI base units.
parts.working: p = F/A; N = kg m s⁻² (C1); kg m s⁻² ÷ m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻² (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express the joule in SI base units.
parts.working: J = N m = kg m s⁻² × m (B1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of quantities have the same SI base units?
A work and power
B momentum and impulse
C force and pressure
D charge and current
parts.working: Momentum kg m s⁻¹; impulse N s = kg m s⁻² × s = kg m s⁻¹. Charge (A s) and current (A) differ by a factor of s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an equation being homogeneous.
parts.answer: Each term in the equation has the same base units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation v² = u² + 2as is homogeneous.
parts.answer: All terms have units m² s⁻².
parts.working: v², u²: (m s⁻¹)² = m² s⁻² (M1); 2as: m s⁻² × m = m² s⁻² (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The pressure p at depth h in a liquid of density ρ is p = ρgh. Show that this equation is homogeneous.
parts.working: ρgh: kg m⁻³ × m s⁻² × m (M1) = kg m⁻¹ s⁻² = unit of p (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the volt.
parts.answer: One joule of energy transferred per coulomb of charge (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the volt is kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹ in SI base units.
parts.working: V = J/C = kg m² s⁻² ÷ (A s) (C1) = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹ (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine the SI base units of resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A small sphere of radius r moving at speed v through a thick oil experiences a drag force F given by F = Crv, where C is a constant. What are the SI base units of C?
A kg s⁻¹
B kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹
C kg m s⁻¹
D kg m⁻² s⁻¹
parts.working: C = F/(rv) = kg m s⁻² ÷ (m × m s⁻¹) = kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹. A forgets to divide by r.

practice.stem: Water flows steadily through a narrow pipe in a hospital drip. The volume flow rate Q is given by Q = πr⁴Δp/(8ηL), where r is the radius of the pipe, L its length, Δp the pressure difference between its ends and η a property of the liquid called viscosity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the SI base units of volume flow rate Q and of pressure difference Δp.
parts.answer: Q: m³ s⁻¹; Δp: kg m⁻¹ s⁻²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the SI base units of η.
parts.working: η = πr⁴Δp/(8QL) (C1); m⁴ × kg m⁻¹ s⁻² ÷ (m³ s⁻¹ × m) = kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ (A1)

practice.stem: The speed v of a transverse wave on a stretched sitar string depends on the tension T in the string and its mass per unit length μ. A student suggests v = k T^x μ^y, where k is a dimensionless constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the SI base units of T and of μ.
parts.answer: T: kg m s⁻²; μ: kg m⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use base units to find the values of x and y.
parts.working: kg: x + y = 0; m: x − y = 1; s: −2x = −1 (M1 for setting up, M1 solving); x = ½, y = −½ (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this method cannot give the value of k.
parts.answer: k is a pure number with no units, so it does not appear in the unit equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student writes s = ut + at² for uniformly accelerated motion. Show that this equation is homogeneous.
parts.working: ut: m s⁻¹ × s = m (M1); at²: m s⁻² × s² = m (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the equation can be homogeneous but still incorrect.
parts.answer: Homogeneity cannot check dimensionless constants; the correct equation has ½at².

parts.label: c
parts.text: The gravitational force between two masses is F = Gm₁m₂/r². Determine the SI base units of G.
parts.working: G = Fr²/(m₁m₂) (C1) = kg m s⁻² × m² ÷ kg² = m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻² (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity.
parts.answer: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
From the list below, state all the vector quantities.
kinetic energy, momentum, temperature, weight, speed, acceleration, power
parts.working: B2 all three and no scalars; B1 two correct

practice.stem: A traveller at Karachi airport pulls a wheeled suitcase with a force of 50.0 N along the handle. The handle makes an angle of 35° with the horizontal floor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal component of the force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the vertical component of the force.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The suitcase moves at constant velocity. State the size of the frictional force on it.
parts.working: Equal and opposite to the horizontal component (B1)

practice.stem: Two horizontal forces act on a crate on a smooth floor: 12.0 N towards the east and 5.0 N towards the north.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force on the crate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle between the resultant force and the east direction.

practice.stem: A light aircraft leaves Islamabad heading due north with a speed of 240 km h⁻¹ relative to the air. A steady wind blows from west to east at 60 km h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the velocity of the aircraft relative to the ground.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the direction of this velocity as an angle from north.
parts.working: tan θ = 60/240 (C1); θ = 14.0° east of north (A1)

practice.stem: A ferry crosses a river 180 m wide. The water flows parallel to the banks at 1.5 m s⁻¹. The speed of the ferry relative to the water is 3.0 m s⁻¹. The ferry must travel straight across, perpendicular to the banks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle between the direction in which the ferry must be steered and the straight-across direction (perpendicular to the banks) so that the ferry moves straight across. State whether the ferry is steered upstream or downstream.
parts.answer: 30° upstream of the straight-across direction (60° to the bank)
parts.working: The upstream component of the ferry's velocity must cancel the current: sin θ = 1.5/3.0 (C1); θ = 30°, steered upstream (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken to cross the river.

practice.stem: A street lamp of weight 30.0 N hangs at rest from two cables tied at the same point. One cable makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal and the other makes an angle of 60° with the horizontal, on the opposite side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the condition for the point where the cables meet to be in equilibrium.
parts.answer: The resultant force on it is zero (the horizontal components balance and the vertical components balance).
parts.working: B1 resultant (vector sum of) force zero

parts.label: b
parts.text: By resolving forces horizontally and vertically, determine the tension in each cable.
parts.answer: Cable at 40°: 15.2 N; cable at 60°: 23.3 N
parts.working: Horizontal: T₁ cos 40° = T₂ cos 60° (C1); vertical: T₁ sin 40° + T₂ sin 60° = 30.0 (C1); solving T₂ = 23.3 N (A1); T₁ = 15.2 N (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the best estimate of the kinetic energy of a family car travelling on a motorway?
A 10³ J
B 10⁴ J
C 10⁶ J
D 10⁸ J
parts.working: m ≈ 1500 kg, v ≈ 30 m s⁻¹: E = ½ × 1500 × 30² ≈ 7 × 10⁵ J ≈ 10⁶ J. 10⁴ J would correspond to a speed of only about 4 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write each quantity in SI units using powers of ten:
(i) 450 nm (ii) 2.5 GHz (iii) 3.3 kΩ (iv) 470 µF
parts.working: B2 all four; B1 two or three

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write 0.000 038 A and 72 000 000 W using a suitable prefix.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the gain in gravitational potential energy of a student who runs up one flight of stairs between two floors of a school building. State the values you assume.
parts.working: B1 sensible values (mass 50–80 kg, height 3–4 m); B1 mgh in range 1.5–3 × 10³ J

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student takes about 4 s. Estimate the useful power output.
parts.working: B1 P = E/t, consistent with (a), in range 300–800 W

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the volume of air in a typical classroom of floor area 8 m × 6 m and height 3 m, and hence its mass. The density of air is 1.2 kg m⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the weight of this air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Most students are surprised by this answer. Suggest why we do not feel the weight of the air in a room.
parts.answer: Air pressure acts in all directions, so the forces on our body from the air balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by rectification.
parts.answer: The conversion of an alternating current (or voltage) into a direct current (one-directional).
parts.working: B1: a.c. → d.c. (current in one direction only).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A single diode is connected in series with a resistor across a sinusoidal a.c. supply. Describe the variation with time of the pd across the resistor.
parts.answer: Positive half-cycles of the sine wave appear; during the negative half-cycles the pd is zero.
parts.working: B1: half-cycles of one polarity only (same shape as input); B1: zero for alternate half-cycles (diode reverse-biased).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name given to this type of rectification and one disadvantage of it.
parts.answer: Half-wave rectification; output is zero for half the time (large ripple, less power).
parts.working: B1: half-wave; B1: no output for half of each cycle / mean power only half / needs large smoothing capacitor.

practice.stem: Four ideal diodes D1–D4 form a bridge rectifier. The a.c. supply is connected between points P and Q. A load resistor R is connected between points X and Y. The diodes are connected as follows: D1 from P to X, D2 from Q to X, D3 from Y to Q, D4 from Y to P (each diode conducts in the direction stated, e.g. D1 allows current from P to X only).

parts.label: a
parts.text: During the half-cycle when P is positive with respect to Q, state which two diodes conduct, and the direction of the current in R (from X to Y or from Y to X).
parts.answer: D1 and D3; from X to Y
parts.working: B1: D1 (P→X) and D3 (Y→Q); B1: current X to Y.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During the next half-cycle, when Q is positive with respect to P, state which two diodes conduct and the direction of the current in R.
parts.answer: D2 and D4; still from X to Y
parts.working: B1: D2 (Q→X) and D4 (Y→P); B1: current still X to Y.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of this type of rectification and describe the waveform of the pd across R.
parts.answer: Full-wave rectification; a series of positive humps with no gaps — every half-cycle appears with the same polarity.
parts.working: B1: full-wave; B1: both halves of each cycle give output of the same polarity (|sin| shape).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the condition relating the time constant RC of the smoothing circuit to the period T of the a.c. supply for good smoothing.
parts.answer: RC must be much greater than T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this condition is needed.
parts.answer: So that only a small fraction of the charge leaks away between peaks, keeping the fall in pd (ripple) small.
parts.working: B1: capacitor discharges very little in one period; B1: pd remains close to peak value — small ripple.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For a 50 Hz half-wave supply and a load of 2.0 kΩ, suggest a suitable minimum capacitance, explaining your choice.
parts.answer: About 100 µF or more (RC = 0.2 s, ten times the 20 ms period).
parts.working: B1: period 20 ms; B1: choose C so RC ≥ about 10T, e.g. C ≥ 100 µF (accept other justified values).

parts.label: a
parts.text: One diode in a bridge rectifier breaks and becomes an open circuit. Describe and explain the effect on the output waveform.
parts.answer: The output becomes half-wave: one set of half-cycles is lost because the current path for those half-cycles goes through the broken diode.
parts.working: B1: half-wave output (every other hump missing); B1: in that half-cycle the conducting pair includes the faulty diode, so no complete circuit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of this fault on the ripple of the smoothed output, giving a reason.
parts.answer: Ripple increases (about doubles) because the capacitor discharges for twice as long between peaks.

practice.stem: An ideal diode is connected in series with a 1.5 kΩ resistor to a sinusoidal supply of peak voltage 6.0 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak current in the resistor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the fraction of each cycle for which there is a current in the resistor, and explain why.
parts.answer: One half; the diode conducts only when forward biased, i.e. during one half-cycle.
parts.working: B1: half; B1: diode has (near) infinite resistance when reverse biased.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The diode is reversed. State the effect on the output.
parts.answer: The other half-cycles are passed: the pd across the resistor is now negative (opposite polarity) during the other half-cycles.
parts.working: B1: output of opposite polarity in the alternate half-cycles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a mobile phone charger must rectify the mains supply before it can charge the battery.
parts.answer: The battery needs current in one direction to store energy chemically; alternating current would charge and discharge it in turn, giving no net charging.
parts.working: B1: charging requires one-way (d.c.) current; B1: a.c. reverses direction every half-cycle so average charge flow is zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why a smoothing capacitor is also included.
parts.answer: To reduce the variation (ripple) of the output so that electronic circuits receive a nearly steady pd.

practice.stem: A capacitor is connected in parallel with the load resistor of a rectifier circuit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the capacitor smooths the output pd.
parts.answer: As the rectified pd rises, the capacitor charges to the peak value; when the rectified pd falls below the capacitor pd, the diode stops conducting and the capacitor discharges through the load, keeping the pd high until the next peak recharges it.
parts.working: B1: capacitor charges as rectified pd rises (to peak); B1: when input falls, capacitor discharges through the load resistor (diode reverse biased so it cannot discharge back through the supply); B1: discharge is slow (time constant ≫ period), so pd falls only a little before the next peak.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the ripple of (i) increasing the capacitance, (ii) increasing the load resistance.
parts.answer: (i) ripple decreases; (ii) ripple decreases — both increase the time constant RC so the capacitor discharges more slowly.
parts.working: B1: both reduce ripple; B1: larger RC → slower discharge.

practice.stem: A half-wave rectifier fed from a 50 Hz supply gives a peak output of 12.0 V. It is smoothed by a 2200 µF capacitor and the load resistance is 1.0 kΩ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the smoothing circuit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume the capacitor discharges for a full period of the supply between peaks. Calculate the minimum pd across the load.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence state the peak-to-peak ripple voltage.

practice.stem: A bridge rectifier is connected to an a.c. supply of r.m.s. voltage 9.0 V. Each conducting diode has a constant pd of 0.70 V across it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak value of the a.c. input.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the peak output is less than the peak input, and calculate the peak output.
parts.working: B1: two diodes conduct in series in each half-cycle, each dropping 0.70 V; A1: 12.7 − 1.40 = 11.3 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A capacitor is added across the load so that the output is well smoothed. State the approximate output pd and the frequency of the ripple when the supply frequency is 50 Hz.
parts.working: B1: approximately the peak output; B1: full-wave → ripple frequency 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

practice.stem: A rectified and smoothed output from a 50 Hz supply is displayed on an oscilloscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the frequency of the ripple for (i) half-wave and (ii) full-wave rectification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The time-base of the oscilloscope is set at 5.0 ms per division. Calculate the number of divisions between successive peaks of the full-wave output.
parts.working: Period of ripple = 10 ms (M1 implied); 10/5.0 = 2.0 div (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Y-gain is 2.0 V per division. The smoothed full-wave trace varies between 4.3 and 4.0 divisions above the zero line. Calculate the peak-to-peak ripple voltage and the mean output voltage (assume the ripple is a symmetrical sawtooth).

practice.stem: The output of a smoothed rectifier varies between a maximum of 8.6 V and a minimum of 7.9 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of the smoothed output waveform over one ripple cycle.
parts.answer: A short steep rise as the capacitor recharges near each peak, followed by a longer, gradual (exponential) fall as it discharges through the load.
parts.working: B1: brief charging near peak; B1: longer slow exponential decay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the peak-to-peak ripple and express it as a percentage of the maximum output.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the charge on the capacitor at the peak that flows away through the load before the next recharge.

practice.stem: A rectified output is smoothed by a capacitor connected across a load resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the following changes, state whether the ripple increases, decreases or stays the same, giving a reason: (i) replacing a half-wave rectifier by a full-wave rectifier; (ii) connecting a second identical load resistor in parallel with the first; (iii) increasing the supply frequency from 50 Hz to 400 Hz.
parts.working: (i) B1 decreases, B1 capacitor discharges for half as long between peaks; (ii) B1 increases, B1 load resistance halves, so RC halves and discharge is faster; (iii) B1 decreases, B1 shorter time between peaks so less discharge.

practice.stem: A 50 Hz supply is rectified to give a peak of 9.0 V across a 1.0 kΩ load smoothed by a 1000 µF capacitor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ripple voltage for half-wave rectification, assuming the capacitor discharges for one whole period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ripple voltage for full-wave rectification.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the ratio of your answers.
parts.answer: About 2 : 1 — full-wave halves the ripple, because the discharge time is halved (and RC ≫ T so the fall is nearly linear).

practice.stem: A full-wave rectifier connected to a 50 Hz supply gives a peak output of 15 V across a 470 Ω load. A smoothing capacitor is to be connected across the load.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time between successive peaks of the rectified output.
parts.working: B1: full-wave → two peaks per cycle → 1/100 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the capacitor discharges for this whole time, calculate the minimum capacitance that keeps the ripple to no more than 5% of the peak pd.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the actual ripple will be slightly smaller than this calculation suggests.
parts.answer: The capacitor starts recharging before the next peak, so it discharges for slightly less than 0.010 s.
parts.working: B1: discharge time is less than the full interval between peaks.

practice.stem: A sinusoidal supply of peak voltage 20 V is rectified and connected to a 100 Ω resistor. The diodes are ideal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean power in the resistor with full-wave rectification (no smoothing).
parts.working: Full-wave output has the same r.m.s. value as the sine wave: V_rms = 20/√2 = 14.1 V (M1); P = V²/R = 2.0 W (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mean power with half-wave rectification is half of this, and calculate it.
parts.working: B1: output is zero for half of each cycle and identical otherwise, so the energy per cycle is halved; A1: 1.0 W.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the r.m.s. voltage of the half-wave rectified output.

practice.stem: An oscilloscope shows the output of a full-wave rectifier (50 Hz supply) smoothed by a capacitor, across a 2.0 kΩ load. During each discharge the pd falls from 10.0 V to 9.2 V in 8.5 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the smoothing circuit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance of the smoothing capacitor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the discharge lasts 8.5 ms rather than the full 10 ms between peaks.
parts.answer: The rectified input rises above the capacitor pd before the peak, so recharging starts early.
parts.working: B1: capacitor begins to recharge before the next peak.
